description: Main stage keynote and presentation talks delivered at DEF CON 34.

talks.title: Hacking AI
talks.teaser: Bruce Schneier examines how artificial intelligence systems hack human institutions, tax codes, financial markets, and legal frameworks.
talks.summary:
Cryptographer and security technologist Bruce Schneier delivers a keynote exploring the multifaceted dynamics of artificial intelligence and security on the Main Stage at DEF CON 34 [00:07]. Schneier structures his analysis around three key axes: humans hacking AI models, humans using AI as an offensive capability, and autonomous AI systems discovering and exploiting systemic vulnerabilities across both technological and human institutions [08:41].

Schneier broadens the traditional concept of hacking beyond software, illustrating how AI systems will systematically uncover and exploit loopholes within tax codes, financial regulations, and democratic processes [17:28]. He explores the "genie problem," where autonomous optimization algorithms inadvertently subvert human intent to satisfy poorly constrained objectives [08:44], proposing that legislative bodies and watchdog groups use AI for predictive red-teaming to discover loopholes in draft bills prior to passage [27:04]. The lecture examines the security realities of "instant software," where generative models dynamically synthesize transient code on demand, requiring fundamental shifts in automated vulnerability analysis and trust models [36:11].

talks.title: Stalking the Wily Hacker: 40 Years Later
talks.teaser: Cliff Stoll reflects on the 40th anniversary of tracking down an international KGB cyber espionage ring originating from a 75-cent accounting error.
talks.summary:
In this historic and captivating keynote from the DEF CON 34 Main Stage, astronomer, author, and cybersecurity pioneer Cliff Stoll takes the stage to reflect on the 40th anniversary of his legendary investigation chronicled in "The Cuckoo's Egg." Opening at 00:04 to an electrifying standing ovation, Cliff recounts how an innocent 75-cent accounting discrepancy in 1986 at the Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory unraveled a sophisticated international cyber espionage ring selling stolen Western military secrets to the Soviet KGB.

At 14:00, Cliff explores the scientific mindset and the gritty realities of research, humorously sharing how amateur curiosity and sheer stubbornness triumph when an investigator is underfunded and bewildered. At 28:01, he recounts working alongside early federal investigator Mike Gibbons, navigating an indifferent intelligence bureaucracy that had never previously encountered network-borne espionage.

At 42:03, Cliff delivers an impassioned critique of sanitizing corporate jargon like "threat actors," urging the audience to maintain personal responsibility and human empathy. He concludes at 56:02 by looking ahead to the future of technology, inspiring attendees to embrace playful curiosity, question dogmas, and celebrate the timeless human spark of hacking. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: BLE Theft Auto - Anti Theft System Exposes Over 1M Cars
talks.teaser: Shows how an aftermarket dealer-installed car alarm shipped one shared key across its units, letting a smartphone unlock and immobilize vehicles.
talks.summary:
The researchers from UC San Diego began with an unrelated study of Bluetooth credit card skimmers at gas pumps. Their scans kept picking up an unfamiliar device, and an FCC filing identified it as KARR, an aftermarket anti-theft system that dealers install and offer as a paid upgrade. The team then studied six aftermarket Bluetooth systems in total and reported that three had serious flaws.

The Android app turned out to be a .NET application packed into a compressed assemblies blob, which hid its Bluetooth code from standard APK analysis. The authentication was a challenge-response scheme, but one ingredient, the secret key, was hard-coded and shared by every unit. Access control existed only in the app's interface, because the server simply listed which vehicles a user could see. Even in the disabled no-sale mode, the device still accepted a mode-change command, which let an attacker restore full control. The demo showed door unlocking, immobilizer disabling, and horn and light triggering.

The vendor later removed the universal key from the app and issued per-vehicle keys, and disabling the unit in no-sale mode now appears to turn it off fully. The team also described a remote starter system whose pairing QR code was built from a public MAC address, and a dealer-linked product they could not fully assess. Their takeaways: aftermarket devices sit outside OEM security reviews, Bluetooth's built-in pairing does not cover vehicle control, and owners with KARR should check for a window sticker and apply the update.

talks.title: Bird Hunting Season - The Final Flight
talks.teaser: Walks through a self-funded teardown of Flock Safety gunshot detectors, license plate readers and edge compute boxes, from UART access to exposed camera feeds.
talks.summary:
This talk closes a multi-year, self-funded research project on Flock Safety surveillance hardware, bought secondhand on eBay. The devices covered are Raven gunshot detectors, Falcon and Sparrow license plate readers, and Picard and Bravo edge compute boxes. The speaker traces the path from physical access over UART and an unauthenticated download mode to weak boot protections, broken mutual TLS, hardcoded keystore secrets, and a root-level log cleanup routine that could be abused for command injection.

The middle section covers the most significant new finding. Internet-wide scanning data showed live camera feeds and admin services reachable without authentication over a cellular data connection. The speaker expanded the search by checking the network block that owned those addresses, which turned up dozens of listings. Another chain used a three-press button sequence to open a hotspot with a shared default password, then moved from a wireless connection to a root shell. The speaker also described a "flea market supply chain" idea: contacting component makers or using vendor tooling can yield SDKs far faster than reverse engineering alone.

The talk ends with BirdShot, a public toolkit of more than a dozen modules that automates several of these chains, and BirdEye, a harness for running a vision model against camera or webcam input. The takeaways are that surveillance devices often ship with debugging enabled, no secure boot or disk encryption, and an assumption of physical isolation that fails once they reach the internet. The speaker also urged people to inventory the surveillance technology around them.

talks.title: C2YA - Inside the Adversary's Inbox
talks.teaser: Shows how LLM-assisted research turned five open-source C2 frameworks into a source of flaws that defenders can use against attacker infrastructure.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a simple question: if coding agents can find bugs in ordinary software, what do they find in the tools attackers use? The speaker pointed LLM-assisted research at five open-source command-and-control frameworks, Havoc, Mythic, Sliver, Covenant and AdaptixC2, several of which have appeared in operations by state-linked and criminal groups. Over about six months the work produced roughly 250 flaws, many reachable from the internet without prior access, each scored by how useful it is to a defender rather than how much damage it does to a target.

The middle covers the most useful bug classes. Havoc reused an AES-CTR keystream for each agent, so XORed ciphertexts leak plaintext through crib dragging, and its unauthenticated WebSocket hands out the session key. Adaptix embedded its RC4 key in every implant, Sliver kept key material in unencrypted SQLite, and Covenant let a low-privilege user read password hashes and escalate to code execution. A live demo eavesdropped on a Havoc team server knowing only its address. A survey of 35 exposed servers, 13 of them live, found a Havoc campaign against French victims that used layered obfuscation and unprotected cloud buckets.

The closing point is that Havoc was archived in February 2026, so its bugs will not be patched and defenders must carry that load. Taking down a C2 server is rarely enough, because operators leave backup access. Practitioners should treat adversary tooling as software worth auditing, both for fingerprinting and traffic decryption and for recognising that attackers may exploit the same flaws.

talks.title: Breaking Local AI Runtimes - Exploiting llama cpp and Ollama
talks.teaser: Walks through three native-code memory bugs in llama.cpp and Ollama, from an Android JNI use-after-free to a Go/C out-of-bounds heap read.
talks.summary:
The talk treats local AI inference runtimes such as llama.cpp and Ollama as ordinary native code, where memory management happens outside the language safety that surrounds it. The presenters split their research across three trust boundaries: the JNI bridge used by Android apps, the HTTP server's model lifecycle, and the Go-to-C interface inside Ollama. They stress that the work is about exploiting the runtime itself, not prompt injection.

On Android, a race between model unload and a benchmark routine leaves a freed context in use. The team reclaims the freed allocation with attacker-chosen contents, redirects a virtual call, and demonstrates code execution inside the host app. In the llama.cpp server, an idle-unload feature can free a model while request handlers still hold a pointer to its vocabulary. They reclaim that chunk remotely across threads and reach an attacker-controlled dereference, but stop short of full remote code execution because they still lack an address leak to defeat ASLR. In Ollama, crafted GGUF tensor shapes make quantization read past a Go-backed buffer. By choosing a conversion path that preserves data, the leaked heap contents survive into the saved model.

The practical takeaways are to avoid idle unloading on exposed servers, place authenticated TLS proxies in front of them, validate every size read from a model file, and use checked arithmetic. Audit unsafe and cgo boundaries for the same patterns. Vendor responses were uneven, and some upstream patches were closed, so the speakers published their fixes.

talks.title: Certified Re-Pwned - Escalating All the Way Up
talks.teaser: Presents five new Active Directory Certificate Services escalation techniques that take a domain user to krbtgt extraction on a fully patched Windows Server 2025 CA.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that Active Directory Certificate Services is still exploitable despite Microsoft's 2022 strong certificate binding enforcement and the 2024 CVE fix. The presenters introduce five new techniques, numbered ESC18 through ESC22 to extend the public ESC1 to ESC17 scheme. Each was validated on a fully patched Windows Server 2025 enterprise CA with Microsoft's recommended mitigations applied. Every chain starts from an ordinary domain user with no special ACL, GPO, or template rights and ends with extraction of the krbtgt key.

The techniques target different parts of the post-2022 defences. One abuses certificate policy identifiers that the CA copies from the CSR into issued certificates, linked to security groups through Authentication Mechanism Assurance. Another injects a security extension that the CA passes through unchecked. A third omits the security extension entirely, which makes the KDC fall back to reading the SID from the SAN URL, an undocumented behaviour. A fourth abuses enrollment on behalf of with version 1 templates, whose array signature attribute the CA silently ignores. The last shows that enrollment agent restrictions can appear configured while being absent, because the certutil flag is not recognised on Server 2025. Each technique was demonstrated live.

For defenders, the recommendations include removing the security extension from the CSR whitelist, enforcing explicit EKUs, disabling the ESS flag where it is not needed, upgrading version 1 templates, restricting enrollment to specific groups, and verifying enrollment agent restrictions in both the GUI and the registry. Suggested detections include event 4887 for security extension object IDs and event 4768 for PKINIT authentication without that extension.

talks.title: Breaking the Ethereum Phone - From BootROM to Wallet Signing Keys
talks.teaser: Shows how a crypto phone's MediaTek boot chain can be patched in memory from bootrom onward, and how the lock-screen and wallet keys behind it can be recovered.
talks.summary:
This talk uses the Ethereum phone (dGEN1) as a case study of "crypto phones", devices that promise to keep wallet keys in hardware-backed storage. The speaker frames the trade-off between browser wallets, which are convenient but exposed to any privileged attacker, and hardware wallets, which are secure but awkward to use. Airdrop incentives make these phones attractive targets. Because root access is not available, the research starts with the MediaTek download mode, where the authentication fuses were found unblown, so a modified preloader could be loaded over USB.

The middle of the talk covers the boot chain. The speaker describes a technique called Loader-of-the-Loader, which patches each later stage in memory so that flash is never written and a failed attempt can be retried. The chain reaches the secure-world hypervisor, ARM trusted firmware and a little kernel, where the image-loading path was replaced and signature checks were bypassed. On the Android side, the screen-lock check runs in a software gatekeeper that reports itself as hardware-backed. Its inputs sit in the password file, so the PIN can be brute-forced offline. The wallet's signing key is a P256 key that controls an on-chain smart account, and the speaker verified that the recovered key matches that account.

The final part looks at the airdrop claim, which relies on a hash of the IMEI and serial number. The speaker showed that two identifiers printed on the retail box were enough to claim rewards for a sealed, unactivated device. The practical lesson is that hardware-backed claims need real secure-element verification, and identifiers printed on packaging should never serve as secrets.

talks.title: Beyond the Ceremony - The 2026 Passkey Attack Surface
talks.teaser: Maps passkey attack surface across authenticators, cross-device transport, browsers, relying parties and cloud sync, with a Burp extension to test them.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the premise that the WebAuthn ceremony is cryptographically sound, but that real passkey deployments rarely rely on it alone. Passkeys usually sit beside weaker sign-in methods, and the login depends on many parts: the authenticator, the transport between devices, the browser, the relying party server, cloud sync, and account recovery. The speaker organizes the scattered research into one map of these components and treats each attack as a stop that still works after a correct ceremony.

Along the way, the talk covers management interfaces exposed by the CTAP cross-device protocol, relay attacks on the QR-code hybrid flow, and client-side tricks such as redirecting ceremonies through malicious extensions or XSS. Most of the time is spent on the server side, where tampering with client data, origin, relying party ID, signatures, algorithms and credential IDs can be tested. A cited study found all 103 live relying parties vulnerable to at least one server-side attack. The speaker also shows Passkey Editor, a Burp extension that decodes vendor-specific encodings and applies preset attacks, demonstrated against WebAuthn.io and GitHub.

The closing sections cover cloud sync, where weak account protection can undermine a passkey, and the interpersonal threat of a partner or family member with access to a shared device. The practical takeaway is that server-side checks form a finite checklist to run quickly, leaving time for business-logic testing. The tool is available for testing passkey deployments.

talks.title: Defender’s Dilemma Releasing Dual-Use AI Models as Capabilities Climb
talks.teaser: Panelists debate how to evaluate and release dual-use AI models, weighing open-weights diffusion and defender advantage as capabilities climb.
talks.summary:
The panel opens by asking whether dual-use AI resembles earlier fights over encryption and export controls. Speakers argue that the central question is who decides which users get access, and they compare AI to telephones, cars and airplanes to show how different mental models lead to different levels of concern. A recurring theme is that friction, including limits on availability, built-in safeguards, legal consequences and defender action, has historically managed dual-use risk.

The middle section covers diffusion. Participants expect capable open-weight models to trail frontier systems by only months, helped by falling token costs and local hardware. They discuss whether coordinated disclosure still works when findings spread instantly, and they point to AI-assisted cryptanalysis and firmware diffing as examples of capabilities that already exist. Alignment, meaning whether a model recognizes when it is in the wrong situation, is raised as a gap in how capability is currently measured.

The closing segment looks at defense. Suggestions include intent-based access decisions, graduated verification instead of yes-or-no checks, audit frameworks that regulators can converge on, and treating integrity as a neglected security property. The practical advice is to press vendors to adopt AI-assisted defense now, prepare for a difficult stretch of roughly eighteen to twenty-four months, and keep contributing ideas to the community.

talks.title: A Provider for the MOFia - Distributed Post Ex Capabilities
talks.teaser: Shows how to install custom WMI providers on a remote Windows host over DCOM and run post-exploitation tasks inside WMIPrvSE without dropping files via SMB or WinRM.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a narrow view of offensive WMI. Most activity centers on Win32_Process Create and event subscriptions, and defenders already watch both closely. The speaker argues that WMI's provider architecture is largely unexplored and presents it as a way to run post-exploitation work from inside the WMI host process.

The central technique is installing a WMI provider on a remote machine without staging files over SMB or WinRM. The speaker reimplemented the parts of mofcomp that parse MOF files and register providers, then serialized the objects in the MS-WMIO binary format and sent them over DCOM. Because WMI has no native file transfer, the talk describes using Desired State Configuration classes to write files and an existing PowerShell v3 class to read them. It also explains that the hosting model sets the privilege a provider runs with, and that removal must follow a fixed order to avoid leaving artifacts in the WMI database.

The speaker released two tools: a WMI-only client for file and process operations, and a provider installer that deploys modules for assembly and BOF execution, token and Kerberos work, and browser cookie access. Demonstrations covered installing and removing providers. Detection ideas include event ID 63 for system-level hosting models, registry writes made through standard RegProv, DSC logging, PowerShell script block logging, and unsigned DLLs in the WBEM directory.

talks.title: Can AI do novel security research - Meet the HTTP Terminator
talks.teaser: Shows how an autonomous AI pipeline invented new HTTP desync triggers, exploited live websites with them, and where human research still adds value.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether an autonomous system can invent new HTTP desync attack techniques and then use them against live websites. Desync research was chosen because each candidate can be proven on a real target instead of remaining a theory. The pipeline has four stages: generating hypotheses from fragments of RFC text, testing candidate triggers across roughly 30,000 bug bounty sites using plain code rather than AI, weaponizing confirmed hits, and feeding each discovery back in to seed further discoveries.

The generator produced about 30,000 unique vectors from 138 RFCs, and several of them caused desync on production systems, including banks and an airport. Early attempts showed that coding agents struggled to build working exploits, so success checks were moved into deterministic code and each stage received only evidence from the previous one. A technique that omits one byte from a second request removed the race condition behind stacked responses. Later cascades produced a zero-day in Apache Traffic Server and a proposed class called shared parser confusion, where servers reuse response-processing code for requests.

The main takeaway is that automated research can surface new issues, but the largest gains came when a human guided the cascade stages. Evaluation design decides whether results are signal or noise. The speaker suggests choosing topics where automated checking is hard if you want to avoid collisions with AI-driven researchers. The full source code of the system has been published.

talks.title: BTR Reforged - Weaponizing Defender's Remediation Driver as a Kernel Operation Primitive
talks.teaser: Reverses the undocumented, encrypted instruction format of a Microsoft-signed Windows Defender driver and turns it into a kernel file and registry operation engine.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with an incident response case. Responders found a service key pointing to a randomly named .sys file whose alternate data stream held its configuration, and first suspected a rootkit. It turned out to be the Boot-Time Removal driver (btr.sys), a Microsoft-signed component that Defender extracts from mpengine.dll only when a remediation needs a reboot. The driver has no IOCTL interface, so its only input is the encrypted configuration stored in that stream.

The speaker documents the format from scratch. The configuration uses RC4 with a 256-byte key that is identical across 18 driver builds spanning roughly Windows 7 to Windows 11, and its integrity checks use a CRC32 variant without the final XOR. The structure has a global header, a feedback file path, and item headers that map to six action IDs covering file deletion, directory deletion, move/quarantine, and registry key, value and set operations. Two actions are especially useful beyond their intended purpose: a move with an empty destination deletes a file, and a move with a valid destination writes without restriction. The companion tool BTR_CLI builds valid transactions and can run them either at runtime or during early boot, in a window before Defender's user-mode services start. The demo removes Defender binaries and registry keys despite tamper protection, then writes a file into a system directory.

The main takeaway for defenders is that no exploit or CVE is involved, and Microsoft did not plan a servicing fix after the report. Detection suggestions include Sysmon events for alternate data stream creation, driver loads paired with file deletions, and tightening the Load Driver privilege.

talks.title: Bring Your Own EDR Breaking Windows Process Protection to build EDR Protected Malware
talks.teaser: Shows how a local administrator can abuse an EDR's own installer and COM dump interface to run unsigned code inside Protected Process Light.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that endpoint detection and response products, which shield themselves with Protected Process Light and tamper protection, can be turned against the systems they guard. The speaker reviews how EDRs use user-mode hooks and kernel callbacks, and why older bypasses such as unhooking, direct syscalls, living-off-the-land binaries and vulnerable drivers have become less reliable.

The focus then moves to SentinelOne. An exposed COM helper's dump method checked only that the caller was an administrator, not who the caller was or where it ran from, so any local admin could dump protected processes. Pairing that with publicly documented techniques for remote COM calls and for mapping a PE into memory, the speaker got a statically linked payload running inside Microsoft Defender, and a demo showed it encrypting files in a folder. A rogue installation path was also described: the site token check ran inside a temporary DLL that could be extracted, and a crafted Base64 JSON value passed it.

The speaker reported that the same access let the injected code block removal of the EDR and tamper with other protected security products, and that similar behavior was seen on CrowdStrike. The issues were disclosed through HackerOne. The main takeaways are that patching a symptom, such as removing user-mode pages from kernel dumps, does not fix the underlying trust problem, and that unexpected security software on a machine deserves the same scrutiny as malware.

talks.title: Bring Your Own Root Of Trust
talks.teaser: Shows how a roughly $45 FPGA can impersonate a discrete SPI TPM on Windows 11 and sit between a real TPM and the motherboard, challenging hardware trust assumptions.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with what a hardware root of trust is for: verifying boot code, measuring what ran, storing keys, and attesting platform state. The speakers separate external root-of-trust chips, which sit on the motherboard, from internal ones built into the processor package. They argue that an external chip is the easier target, and they describe NVIDIA DPU boards that use a Microchip external root of trust. One board had a test-bypass pin that could be reached with a fine wire under the package, which they said they had not fully tested on the target hardware.

For the second part, they set out to build a cheap stand-in for a discrete SPI TPM. Microcontrollers were too slow to answer the bus in time, so they moved to small FPGA boards. A low-cost Tang Nano board first ran as a minimal TPM that reported only static PCR values, and Windows accepted it. A later version sat between a real TPM and a motherboard with a logic analyzer, and it forced PCR extends to a fixed value while passing every other command through. Windows still rejected the setup for BitLocker because it checks the TCG event log. Most of the Verilog was written with an AI assistant, which the speakers presented as the main change in who can attempt this work.

The closing takeaway is that the required hardware costs tens to a few hundred dollars. Attackers could use this to spoof hardware identity, fake PCR state for measured boot, or probe attestation. The speakers note that early boot measurements are harder to forge, and that anti-cheat systems detected their test setup. They say the code, gateware, prompts, and data are being released for others to reproduce.

talks.title: Breaking Hardware CFI with Sigreturn
talks.teaser: Shows how sigreturn can bypass ARM64 BTI and PAC on Linux and Android, and how it chains with COOP and coroutine attacks for code execution.
talks.summary:
This talk examines whether hardware control-flow integrity on 64-bit ARM Linux and Android, pointer authentication for return addresses and branch target identification for indirect jumps, can be bypassed through the signal return path. The presenter explains that sigreturn restores the saved processor state, including the branch-type field that BTI checks. By crafting a signal frame with that field zeroed, an attacker can land on ordinary code gadgets without a valid landing pad.

Because forged frames must sit on the stack, the attack needs a bootstrap. The talk introduces CFI-safe stack pivots that begin on a valid landing pad, using a glibc context function and a statically linked unwinder inside Android's Bionic library. Chained frames then loop through gadgets and sigreturn calls. The presenter also shows composition with COOP, which abuses C++ virtual calls, and with C++20 coroutine frames, whose resume pointer can be overwritten. This reduces the need to control the first argument and cuts the memory used by the frames.

A live demo on an Ubuntu server on AWS ARM hardware with BTI and PAC enabled used a heap overflow to scan a 256 KB buffer for a random secret, which the exploit then recovered. The practical takeaway is that BTI and PAC do not close these reuse paths on current Linux systems, and the presenter suggests the issue may be hard to fix.

talks.title: Breaking Amazon lockers by any means necessary
talks.teaser: Follows a researcher's multi-angle attempt to defeat Bluetooth-operated Amazon lockers, from BLE protocol reversing to firmware extraction and physical lock work.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a practical question: Bluetooth Low Energy lockers hold millions of parcels, and porch thefts make them look like a safer option. The speaker began by scanning a locker's advertising data and GATT characteristics, then recorded phone-to-locker traffic in Wireshark. Comparing repeated pickups while changing one variable at a time, he mapped a CBOR-style message format, found a timestamp that worked against replay, and identified the packet that opened a slot. Forging that command failed, because the locker and the app perform mutual public-key authentication.

He then shifted to the phone side. Intercepting the app's traffic and bypassing certificate pinning showed that the open command and session credentials come from Amazon's servers, but the locker still rejected anything it could not verify. Next came the hardware. Documents and leaked maintenance videos from the manufacturer pointed to a board bought cheaply online, whose firmware had no readout protection, but the firmware turned out to be test code, not the production protocol. Physical attacks on the slot locks followed, including key-pattern analysis and custom key fabrication.

The main takeaway is about persistence across attack surfaces. Each dead end pushed the work toward a different layer, and the talk presents the locker as a case study in why a well-designed cryptographic protocol can still leave the mechanical and manufacturing layers exposed.

talks.title: 8 Out of 10 Banks in Belgium HATE This One Weird eID RCE
talks.teaser: Shows how a Belgian eID signing browser extension let any website read smart card data, leak PIN tokens and reach drive-by code execution.
talks.summary:
The talk examines Connective's signing browser extension, used by many Belgian banks and government bodies, and the native host it relays to. The speaker explains the trust chain: a web page messages the extension, which forwards the request to the native host without recording where it came from. The only gate is an activation token, and because that token carries no origin binding, it can be replayed by any site.

Using a virtual eID and a virtual Maestro card built on an ESP32 board, the researcher showed that any page or iframe could read the full contents of a card. The host also returned a PIN token that held the PIN encrypted with a key included in the same token and an IV hardcoded in the binary. That allowed decryption and reuse for about five minutes, so an attacker could phish a PIN once and then authenticate or sign as the victim. The native host also validated library paths by searching for "DLL" as a substring, so a file with a double extension passed the check and could be downloaded and loaded as a polyglot, giving code execution from an ordinary-looking download.

The vendor first rated the problems medium severity and fixed them months later, after follow-up and a national agency's involvement. The practical takeaways are that extension store reviews focus on malware rather than vulnerabilities, native hosts should be treated as untrusted attack surface, and extension developers must validate input that arrives from web content.

talks.title: 1.1M Cameras, One Wildcard - Architectural Surveillance in an IoT Cloud
talks.teaser: Shows how one MQTT wildcard subscription exposed live camera data from about 1.1 million devices, and how a white-label IoT vendor's cloud leaked its own secrets.
talks.summary:
The talk begins with a simple question from a colleague: is a store-bought baby monitor safe? The speaker found that many camera brands sold on retail sites shared one manufacturer's backend, then reverse engineered the companion Android app. Decompiling it exposed hard-coded peer-to-peer material, a request-signing scheme, a list of device commands and the addresses of the MQTT brokers and a configuration server.

The middle of the talk covers the exposed services. Several EMQX brokers accepted default credentials or anonymous clients, so a wildcard subscription streamed messages from roughly 1.1 million devices in 118 countries. The messages carried motion alerts with image links, device bindings, user email addresses and MAC addresses. An unauthenticated Apollo configuration server returned hundreds of production secrets, including database credentials and a key that allowed rebinding devices to other accounts. Images were stored in shared buckets with no per-customer isolation, and the image encryption was trivially reversible. The speaker also described a back-office portal reachable through employee single sign-on, and a vulnerable job scheduler.

The disclosure process was slow and difficult. The vendor was silent for days, later proposed restrictive terms, and backdated its advisories. Five CVEs were assigned, but the fix mainly moved services behind a firewall, and default credentials still worked on some brokers. The main takeaway is that access was built into the architecture, so patching one component left the attack chain intact.

talks.title: CUDA've done better - Hacking Nvidia GPUs for container escape and privilege escalation
talks.teaser: Shows how a use-after-free in the NVIDIA Linux kernel module lets an unprivileged container user escape to root on the host.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a Pwn2Own NVIDIA category target, the NVIDIA Container Toolkit, and the question of whether a malicious container can run code on the host. The researchers mapped the attack surface: the Go management code, the GPU kernel driver, and the RISC-V GSP firmware. They focused on the open-source Linux kernel module, because containers on one host share a kernel, and found a use-after-free there. The vulnerability itself is not detailed, and NVIDIA had already patched it.

The middle section covers how they made the bug reliable. A freed object can be reclaimed by an allocation whose contents are copied back to user space through the ioctl buffer, which leaks whatever gets written into it. To win the race, they used the read-write semaphore's writer-preference behavior and reordered lock acquisitions so the timing became deterministic. They then corrupted a linked-list node to get an arbitrary unlink, overwrote a memory-mapping structure's start and size fields, and mapped all of physical memory into user space.

A recorded demo shows the exploit run inside a container and return a root shell on the host. The speaker said an AI coding agent wrote much of the final physical-memory exploitation. The takeaway is that a single driver bug can break container isolation when containers share the host kernel, and that GPU driver code deserves the same scrutiny as core kernel code.

talks.title: Forgotten but Not Gone - Unauthenticated RCEs and LPEs in Legacy Linux Services
talks.teaser: Traces unauthenticated RCE and privilege escalation bugs in GNU telnetd and Samba, showing how decades-old Linux services still hide critical flaws.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at legacy Linux network services that get less attention than newer technology. The speaker starts with an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw in GNU telnetd, disclosed earlier this year after about eleven years. The daemon passes client-supplied environment variables into the command line of the login program, and because those values are not sanitized, an attacker can inject options that skip authentication and return a root shell.

The research then follows the same attack surface to a local privilege escalation. Login trusts a credentials directory variable and a flag file inside it, so a low-privilege user can reach root through telnetd even after the first patch. Turning to Samba, the speaker reports two more unauthenticated RCEs. One comes from a printing interface that places a job name into a shell command. The other comes from a password validation RPC call that reaches a command without escaping. Each issue is shown in a live demo.

The takeaway is that narrow patches fix individual instances but leave the flawed design behind them in place. Practitioners should ask whether a service runs shell commands, sanitizes input, or accepts environment variables from unauthenticated clients, and should not assume that popularity means it has been audited. Printers, routers and other unmanaged devices may still run these daemons unpatched.

talks.title: Condense Volumes, Connect Dots - Scaling Root Cause Analysis andTroubleshooting with ML
talks.teaser: Shows how machine learning can group, deduplicate and enrich security logs before SIEM ingestion, cutting volume and stitching alerts into attack stories.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a familiar SOC problem: analysts face thousands of alerts from many tools, and retention and search budgets limit how much history can be correlated. Stitching a multi-month intrusion together across separate platforms is still largely manual. The speaker uses a 2017 healthcare breach as an example, showing how an attack spans a long timeline and many machines, which makes a single correlation search inadequate.

The proposed approach runs before the SIEM. A small, lightweight model tags each record with MITRE ATT&CK techniques and related control references, then clusters related records and orders them by causality into attack flows. The speaker points to highly redundant intrusion detection alerts that differ only in their timestamps, and argues that grouping and deduplicating such records can cut volume by roughly 90 percent without losing data.

The takeaway is partly financial and partly operational. Lower ingest and AI token costs can fund more analysts, and a smaller, enriched dataset gives downstream anomaly detection more useful signal. The project is presented as open source. The speaker notes that teams needing custom filtering rules should still use dedicated pipeline tools, while this approach focuses on the largest reduction gained from grouping.

talks.title: Compounding Interest - Exploiting the ATM Supply Chain
talks.teaser: Shows how a vendor's BitLocker wrapper on ATM disks can be bypassed to recover keys, with nine new CVEs and an open toolkit.
talks.summary:
The talk follows earlier research on Diebold Nixdorf ATMs and turns to the software that protects their disks. Diebold uses CryptoPro Secure Disk for BitLocker, a proprietary layer that adds pre-boot authentication, TPM sealing and an obfuscated encryption scheme on top of Windows BitLocker. Because CryptoPro is sold commercially, the researcher could obtain a recent release and rebuild the setup in a virtual environment.

The middle of the talk covers the analysis. A hidden area of the Linux boot partition holds a layout table that points to an encrypted configuration store, and the researcher reversed the key derivation and cipher used to open it. The TPM secrets were stored in a form that could be read from the offline disk, and the PCR measurements were bound only to a few unencrypted EFI files. The disk-encryption key sits in a further store protected by a key derived from a hardware fingerprint. The flaws that made the attack possible included a fallback that mounts partitions unencrypted when decryption fails, a encryption check that trusts only a four-byte header, and no integrity checks on the store's contents. Two demos showed a rebuilt root filesystem being booted and a live Linux image using a Microsoft-signed shim to get past Secure Boot.

The talk closes with the disclosure timeline. Nine CVEs were reported to the vendor, and the later version 7.7.4 measures boot state before unsealing the TPM and removes the fallback path. The speaker also released Ragavan, a toolkit that automates extraction, decryption, TPM unsealing and BitLocker recovery. The takeaway for practitioners is that a vendor's security wrapper can add its own attack surface to the supply chain.

talks.title: CloudBashing for mining, networking, exfil, persistence
talks.teaser: Reverses the private APIs behind AWS, Azure, and GCP CloudShell to show how unmanaged cloud terminals can be abused for free compute, staging, and persistence.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with what a cloud shell is: a browser terminal attached to a backend container, with a preinstalled CLI and the user's credentials already bound to it. The speakers explain that the work began with a CTF they built for a previous DEF CON, where the flag lived inside a cloud shell. Sniffing the browser traffic led them to reverse the private REST and websocket protocols used by all three major clouds, and to trace how credentials move from console logins to temporary tokens.

The middle of the talk covers what the reversed API makes possible. A terminal tool built on it can provision large numbers of containers from one credential. In AWS, each region gets its own cloud shell, and federation calls that accept arbitrary session names let a single identity create many more, so the speakers reached 160 nodes. Because no CPU metering or billing alert catches this, cryptomining goes unnoticed. The team also showed a file-download path that runs curl inside the container, which could be hijacked to swap in a trojanized script and capture credentials. Storage can be spread across regions, websocket sessions can outlive token revocation through idle-reset pings, and Microsoft device-code flows and free consumer Gmail accounts can reach the service.

The closing takeaways are that these containers are unmanaged, hard to audit, and easy to forget during incident response. The speakers suggest disabling cloud shells where they are not needed, and otherwise treating them as assets that need their own controls and monitoring. They also released a toolkit, CloudBasher, for enumerating and running distributed workloads across these environments.

talks.title: From Fuzzer Noise to Zend Engine 0Day - Exploiting a Heap UAF Across All PHP Vuln
talks.teaser: Follows a mistriaged PHP fuzzer crash from a core Zend use-after-free to a command run on stock PHP despite ASLR and disable_functions.
talks.summary:
The talk begins with a fuzzer report against PHP that was filed under a JIT label, yet the bug reproduces with JIT, opcache and all extensions absent. The speakers trace it to a use-after-free in the core engine's concatenation path, where a destructor triggered during a property write leaves a stale reference behind. They show the defect was already publicly reported and that PHP declined to treat it as a security issue.

The middle of the talk covers turning the crash into a working exploit. A reclaimed object of matching size gives controlled reads and writes, a date-interval technique steers memory access, and the module base is computed from a leaked internal pointer so the system function can be resolved inside the process. The demonstration runs on a distribution build as an unprivileged user with address randomization, PIE and disable_functions enabled. The speakers claim one addition of their own: routing the call through SPL array access rather than calling the function directly. They also say that much of the chain matched earlier public work they found partway through the project.

For defenders, the takeaway is that disable_functions is not an isolation boundary. Process isolation, least privilege and blocking upload or exec footholds matter more. The root cause has a narrow fix, clearing the destination before destroying the old value, which passed their test runs but had not landed upstream at recording time. Sanitizer output showing this free path is a usable detection signal.

talks.title: Fireside Chat
talks.teaser: Presents a fireside conversation on how AI is speeding up offense, why rural water systems need basic defenses, and what DEF CON Franklin aims to achieve.
talks.summary:
The conversation opens with DEF CON Franklin, an initiative to help rural water utilities. The guests describe these operators as underfunded and often located near military bases, and they note that roughly 50,000 water agencies serve most Americans. Default credentials and unpatched internet-facing controllers are still among the easiest ways in, so the focus is on fixing fundamentals first.

The middle of the talk turns to AI. The speaker argues that automated tools can rapidly generate exploits, shrinking the time defenders have to recognize, understand and patch a flaw. They discuss an incident in which AI agents in a test sandbox got out and reached an outside platform, and they consider how capture-the-flag competitions have shifted toward agent-driven play. Open-weight models spreading beyond government reach make regulation harder, and the speakers argue that pressure from automated offense will push companies toward stronger authentication.

The closing takeaways are practical. Measure the exposure across utilities before trying to improve it, train trusted local people who can teach their peers, and bring together government, industry, academia and the hacking community. The speakers admit that failures will happen and that learning from them matters as much as success.

talks.title: DJ Got Us Fallin' in Creds - How Rekordbox Hands Your Entire Hard Drive to the Dance Floor
talks.teaser: Shows how Rekordbox's Pro DJ Link export mode exposes an entire laptop hard drive over NFS to any device on the same subnet.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a DJ, producer and builder of a Twitch now-playing tool, set out to understand Pro DJ Link, the protocol that lets Pioneer and Alpha Theta players talk to each other. While working with it, they found that Rekordbox, the popular DJ software, starts an NFS-based export service when a laptop is linked over the network. That service exposes the whole drive rather than only the music library, and the sole gate is a constant value built into the protocol that the open-source community has known about for years.

Rekordbox also does not restrict which file paths a client may request, so any device on the same subnet that presents that value can read files such as SSH keys, cookies and browser history. The speaker frames this as a confused deputy problem: the authentication behaves as designed, but the software acts with the full rights of the logged-in user. A live demo showed a remote machine listing exported volumes and pulling a file from a user folder with a short script. The affected platforms include the desktop app on Windows and macOS, the mobile apps on Android and iOS, and hardware with a file system. Fixes were staggered, with desktop patches due soon, mobile in August, and hardware firmware expected to take longer.

The obvious fix, hardening the shared credential, is difficult because the value has shipped in firmware since 2009 and changing it would stop existing gear from connecting in clubs. Narrowing the NFS scope to music folders is also nontrivial given libraries of tens of thousands of tracks. Disclosure followed a 90-day timeline coordinated through a community contact. Practical advice is to update Rekordbox, disable Pro DJ Link when it is not needed, and keep sensitive files off USB media used at venues.

talks.title: Franklin - What worked, what didnt, and how we are giving agency to water utilities
talks.teaser: Explains how DEF CON Franklin volunteers and a regional managed security provider network aim to bring basic cybersecurity to under-resourced American water utilities.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces the Water Watch Center, a new entity meant to deliver cybersecurity at scale to American water utilities. The speakers note that about 150,000 utilities want to do security properly but have no staff or budget, and they cannot easily raise rates to pay for it. The proposed structure is meant to act like a nervous system: the National Rural Water Association serves as the hub, while five managed security service providers, one per CISA region with a plan to reach ten, handle day-to-day work and share anonymized data upward.

A volunteer named David describes helping a small town public works department with four employees and no in-house IT. The engagement started with a full assessment and asset inventory, then moved to coordinating with the town's outside vendors and fitting controls to a budget that began at zero. He found that basic hygiene, such as multifactor authentication on public-facing systems, landed best when explained through patient, listening-first conversations. Josh Corman argues that losing water quickly disables hospitals, and describes a parallel effort to engineer resilience for a dozen hospital towns.

In questions, the speakers argued that free vendor products often carry hidden staffing costs, and that some security appliances themselves have exploited vulnerabilities, so technology is not always the answer. The main takeaway is that these utilities lack people more than tools, and that sustained federal funding for the rural water association is needed to keep the model running.

talks.title: DC101
talks.teaser: Gives first-time DEF CON attendees a practical orientation to villages, contests, goons, safety, badges, and how to get involved.
talks.summary:
This DC 101 session is an orientation for first-time attendees at DEF CON's convention center venue. The speakers open by arguing that credentials such as CVEs or certifications do not decide who belongs at the con, and that curiosity and participation matter more. They describe the event as a choose-your-own-adventure: villages and communities run by volunteers, contests, parties, and hallway conversations all compete for limited time. They recommend the Hacker Tracker app for schedules, maps, and room changes, and they urge people to leave time for walking and lines.

The middle of the talk covers people and safety. Goons in red shirts and badges handle navigation, line control, and escalation, with NFO booths and the Hotline available for help. The head of the SOC encourages attendees to fake badges but warns against impersonating goons, and notes that badge life projects can also be security tools. Guidance on the DEF CON wireless network includes avoiding work laptops, keeping traffic encrypted, and remembering that exposed credentials can appear on the Wall of Sheep. The speakers also cover hydration and sleep.

The closing advice is to skip a rigid schedule and spend time in villages, where experts and volunteers are easy to approach. Recorded talks can be watched later, so live-only content such as contests, hands-on labs, and Q&A should take priority. The speakers note that volunteering can lead to goon, village lead, or community roles.

talks.title: Data Tomb Raider - Raiding Modern AI Vaults with Legacy Flaws for Treasure Stealing
talks.teaser: Shows how a one-click URL parameter, classic web bugs and gaps in AI guardrails chain into data theft from Microsoft Copilot and Atlassian Rovo.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the premise that AI assistants now read mailboxes, chats, and company files, so each new feature gives attackers another path in. The presenters describe parameter-to-prompt injection, where a URL parameter on a legitimate assistant page runs as a prompt as soon as a victim clicks the link. They use Microsoft Copilot Personal as the first case and walk through four stages: getting in, collecting data, moving it out, and getting past guardrails. A repeated-request trick got around the filter in their example.

The middle section covers Atlassian's Rovo, where the same entry point led to Confluence, Jira, and Bitbucket content through a research sub-agent that could reach the web. A later case against Microsoft 365 Copilot Enterprise had no direct internet access. The attack relied on HTML injection that rendered while the model was still streaming output, before the sanitizer ran, plus an image request routed through a Bing endpoint allowed by the content security policy. The demos show stolen data reaching an attacker server. The presenters say the vendors fixed the issues after disclosure.

To close, the speakers propose a three-step model for agent attacks: enter, evade, and escape. Teams can use it to map input channels, guardrail bypasses, and exfiltration paths. The main takeaway is to test the seams between old web defenses and new AI behavior, since each control may hold on its own while the combination fails.

talks.title: CRLF Powered Desync Attacks - Beheading HTTP streams
talks.teaser: Shows how CRLF header injection behind NGINX proxies can be escalated into HTTP request smuggling, from cache poisoning to browser-driven account takeover.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a common view that header injection only leads to open redirects or cross-site scripting. The speakers show that an NGINX misconfiguration, where proxy_pass is combined with a decoded URI variable, lets URL-encoded line breaks become real headers and split a single request into two. Using this, they describe response queue poisoning inside a CDN's internal infrastructure, and similar cases on telecom, e-commerce and phone-maker platforms. They also show a single-header variant that yields CL.TE desyncs, and head-request overreads that produce cache poisoning and cross-user XSS.

The middle of the talk covers cases where connections are not shared between users. The speakers use Expect 100-continue to make the proxy over-read responses, then move the desync into the victim's browser. Same-site navigation and iframes deliver the payload, leading to XSS and account takeover. They also cover response header injection, which enables cookie tossing and an XSS on redirect responses by abusing edge cache-control behaviour.

For practitioners, the main takeaway is to avoid decoding NGINX variables such as URI in proxy configuration, and to use HTTP/2 towards the upstream server. The speakers released a Burp extension, Nuclei templates for detection, sample attacker pages and labs for testing the techniques.

talks.title: Crashing the Party - Pwning Control Flow Integrity w SegFault Oriented Programming
talks.teaser: Shows how Linux signal-handling flaws let an attacker chain segfaults into arbitrary code execution that bypasses Intel CET shadow stacks.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a familiar idea: when a program makes an invalid memory access, the kernel delivers a segmentation fault and the process normally dies. The speakers argue that this crash can instead become a controlled loop. They contrast it with code-reuse attacks such as return-oriented and sigreturn-oriented programming, which Intel CET is built to stop, and review the two CET parts: the shadow stack and indirect branch tracking.

The middle section explains Linux signal delivery. A handler is registered with sigaction, the kernel saves register state into a frame on the stack, and sigreturn restores it. The key observation is that the shadow stack pointer is validated only after the frame has already been restored, so a forged frame can still set registers before the fault fires. The presenters combine tricks for controlling handler arguments and pivoting to fake frames, then demonstrate on nginx 1.4.0 with a known overflow and shadow stacks enabled. A backward variant abuses the restorer field to build a recursive shadow stack.

The closing section covers mitigations. The team's patch blocks the backward variant by rejecting restorer values with the top bit set. The forward technique relies on deeper user-to-kernel transition weaknesses, which are harder to fix and will take time. The takeaway is that signal handling is a real gap in hardware CFI, and defenders should watch for kernel changes. Code and the paper are in their repository.

talks.title: Chaining Microsoft binaries to get privileged primitives in Windows kernel
talks.teaser: Revives a PPL injection technique to reach a protected Windows process, then abuses a System Guard kernel driver to freeze Microsoft Defender.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with System Guard Runtime Monitor, a Defender extension built for integrity attestation that has since been disabled and removed from Windows. Its kernel driver, sgrm-agent.sys, routes requests through a single IOCTL dispatcher, and the speaker walks through its routines, including memory mapping and thread freezing. To reach them, a caller must run as a protected process under the broker's service identity and hold the one driver handle the broker opened.

The attack starts inside a protected process. The speaker revives a 2018 technique that abused a COM interface in WerFault Secure, which later Microsoft patches broke. Sideloading a vulnerable faultrep DLL restores that interface, and a shared section passed through a command-line argument lets a crafted thread context call WriteProcessMemory to plant shellcode in a DLL's code section. That shellcode duplicates the broker's driver handle, freezes every thread of the Defender engine for fifteen minutes, then restores them. A demo shows a test file that Defender normally flags going undetected during that window.

For defenders, the talk recommends blocking driver downgrades and vulnerable driver loads, and watching for privileged handle requests to protected processes, which a kernel object callback can strip. The freeze routine was removed in later driver builds, and Windows 11 25H2 no longer ships the driver, though the speaker says the chain can be adapted to load it as a service. Source code is public.

talks.title: Chaining Logical Bugs for Reliable Windows LPE
talks.teaser: Shows how small, individually low-severity Windows logic bugs chain into reliable SYSTEM privilege escalation without any memory corruption.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that modern Windows mitigations have made memory corruption expensive, while logic flaws in privileged services still give dependable privilege escalation. The speaker treats low-severity bugs as reusable primitives, such as deleting a file, killing a process, or creating and deleting a registry key, and then combines them so that one fills the gap left by another.

The first chain links two service-level flaws. A Windows Search plugin reads an attacker-writable state file and deletes a path taken from it without checking for symlinks. A separate error reporting service, started on demand through an event trigger, terminates any process ID it receives without an access check. Restarting Search through a COM object lets the delete fire on demand. The second chain starts from a cloud files kernel driver that creates registry keys owned by the caller because of a missing security flag. A scheduled task that runs as SYSTEM then deletes keys through a followed link, and the result is a performance DLL registry entry that a system collector loads and executes.

Microsoft patched three of the four bugs, mostly by hiding the vulnerable code behind feature flags. The process-kill bug remained unpatched at the time of the talk. The practical takeaway is to look for partial control over a privileged resource, then search for a second primitive that makes it dangerous. Impersonation paths that create objects without an explicit owner also deserve close review.

talks.title: How 2 Researchers Turned Boredom Into a Natl Audit
talks.teaser: Two Polish researchers walk through unauthenticated code execution flaws they found across government websites and the vendor disclosure fights that followed.
talks.summary:
Two Polish penetration testers explain how they spent their spare time checking the security of public-sector websites in Poland. They begin with the legal question, citing a provision in the Polish penal code that exempts people who test a system to secure it, notify the administrator, and cause no harm, while warning that careless testing can still break things.

The first target was PAD-CMS, a content system used for mandatory public information bulletins. It was end-of-life with no patches, and they showed two unauthenticated remote code execution paths, one of which came from loose comparisons and how PHP handles request arrays. A third path was found by another researcher. Later work found a file manager plugin with default empty credentials, a base64 image upload that accepted PHP code, and a court system where roughly 245 of about 300 courts had vulnerable instances. A web application firewall rule that blocked the admin path could be bypassed with a double slash.

The talk closes with common problems: agencies have no software requirements, end-of-life products stay in service, and vendors sometimes deny or downplay flaws, including calling direct database access from a desktop client a security inconvenience. The speakers report reports to national CERT and ministry bodies covering roughly 10,000 agencies and a quarter million websites over about two years. Their advice is to test responsibly and use these skills for public benefit.

talks.title: Gotta Phish 'Em All Novel Attack Techniques via Persistent Browser in the Middle
talks.teaser: Presents persistent browser-in-the-middle phishing attacks that bypass MFA, keep sessions alive after logout, and tamper with downloads, plus an open-source framework.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the limits of current real-time phishing proxies. They drop requests during multi-factor challenges, lose visibility once a victim signs in, and allow little interaction after the initial capture. Browser-in-the-middle addresses this by sharing an attacker-controlled remote browser with the victim, so the victim authenticates inside that browser. The speaker also lists gaps in earlier public proofs of concept, including single-victim design, weak stability, limited modularity, and lost sessions after logout, and explains how the new work addresses them.

The core techniques combine a low-latency streaming layer with dynamic resolution and a replaced cursor, a bidirectional WebSocket channel that can alter page DOM, push JavaScript, or deliver files, and a hardened Firefox kiosk profile. Firefox extensions read cookies and local storage, log keystrokes, rewrite in-flight data, and intercept downloads so a modified file can be sent back. A logout handler clears cookies in the attacker's browser while the victim sees a normal sign-out, so the session stays usable. Live demonstrations cover a Google sign-in, a Drive file swap, a click-fix clipboard delivery, a fake camera prompt, and a fetch-based port scan from the victim's machine.

For defenders, the speaker points to signals such as unusual WebSocket traffic, sign-ins from distant locations within a short time, and client-side DOM changes. Planned work includes real-time password manager spoofing, Chrome support, and AI-driven phishing flows. The open-source release of the core framework, with its dashboard, base modules, and extensions, was announced for after the talk.

talks.title: LGTM Bypassing an LLM Build Gate When Prompt Injection Fails
talks.teaser: Shows how an LLM-based pull request gate guarding OpenSearch CI secrets was bypassed, and why a model cannot verify what it never sees.
talks.summary:
The talk examines an LLM gate that OpenSearch placed in front of its CI pipeline. The gate decides whether a first-time contributor's pull request may trigger a workflow that holds AWS and Docker Hub credentials. The speaker reached it after reporting a pull request target weakness, and the project replied that the model would catch the attack.

The speaker's early attempts failed. Encoded commands, nested base64 layers, and direct prompt injection were all flagged. Analysis of the gate's prompt showed that its output-format instructions discouraged the model from using tools, so it behaved like a single-shot classifier. Hiding a payload in a large diff also failed, and moving the payload into a binary annotation processor was caught because the model judged the artifact by its origin. The working path used the build file itself. The model trusted dependency namespaces it saw in the repository, so a lookalike namespace on Maven Central, tied to a domain the speaker could buy, passed the gate in a small share of runs. That was enough.

The project's fix added a warning about dependency changes to the prompt. The main lesson is that the model only sees the diff. It cannot query registries or check domain ownership, and its non-determinism means a low pass rate is still exploitable. An LLM can be one layer of a defense, but it should not be the only gatekeeper.

talks.title: Harvest Now, Decrypt Later - Practical Attacks on Post Quantum Cryptography Implementations
talks.teaser: Shows how memory corruption, compiler-introduced timing leaks, and fault injection can break post-quantum ML-KEM and ML-DSA implementations today, without a quantum computer.
talks.summary:
The speaker argues that the push to deploy NIST's lattice-based post-quantum standards, ML-KEM and ML-DSA, is opening gaps for ordinary implementation bugs. He says the math is sound, but the code is new, written under migration deadlines, and often lightly audited.

The talk covers three attack classes. First, length-handling mistakes at the deserialization boundary can overflow a stack buffer during a hybrid TLS 1.3 key exchange, which he presents as a route to code execution before any cryptography runs. Second, constant-time C code that uses a branchless bit test was turned into a secret-dependent branch by Clang optimizations, creating a chosen-ciphertext oracle that leaks partial key material over a local network. Third, on a Cortex-M4 target, a voltage glitch that cuts short coefficient sampling during ML-DSA signing leaks the secret vector, demonstrated with a low-cost ChipWhisperer.

He argues that hybrid classical-plus-PQC helps against some of these bugs and not others. Practical defenses include memory-safe parsing and fuzzing, constant-time measurement and verification, and verified implementations. The talk ends with a live run of LatticeScope, an open-source timing-leak detector and structure-aware fuzzer, which flags planted bugs and then runs against a real implementation.

talks.title: Get Set, Exploit - Unveiling Python Class Pollution In the Wild
talks.teaser: Introduces a six-type taxonomy of Python class pollution, an automated static analysis tool, and dozens of zero-day exploits found across popular packages.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with Python's object model, where everything is an object linked by references and dunder attributes. Dynamic reflection such as getattr and setattr lets attacker-supplied keys walk that graph, so a recursive updater can reach classes, modules and secrets far beyond the object it was meant to touch. The speakers trace the history from a 2023 blog post to a 2024 PyTorch Lightning CVE, arguing that those were only the visible part.

The core contribution is a taxonomy built from two get primitives and three set primitives, yielding six pollution types, of which only one was previously known. The team then built Pyrl, which applies a new static analysis called operational taint analysis. Run across more than 600,000 GitHub and PyPI packages, it produced 886 alerts, and the researchers report 47 exploitable zero-days in projects including Azure CLI, Taipy and ComfyUI.

Case studies show how these flaws become serious. In Django Unicorn, an unauthenticated state-update API allowed denial of service, cross-site scripting through BeautifulSoup's sanitization table, forged signing secrets, and remote code execution. A second case, in TypeY, started from a weak constrained primitive and needed a race condition to reach eval. The takeaway for developers is to restrict which attributes can be traversed and to validate the final target before any assignment.

talks.title: Keychained Melody Grabbing the Keys to the iCloud Kingdom
talks.teaser: Shows how a macOS trust flaw let an attacker with code execution pull iCloud Keychain secrets, and how Apple patched it.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with how Apple protects iCloud Keychain. Secrets sync only among devices in a trust structure that has grown from a simple circle into a graph called Octagon, and the keys guarding them are rooted in the Secure Enclave. The presenters argue that infostealers now routinely take local keychains, which makes the iCloud copy the more personal prize. They set out to test whether an attacker already running code on a Mac could reach it.

The core flaw sits in the trusted peers helper daemon, which keeps the list of devices allowed to read the data. By injecting an attacker-generated key pair into that database, the attacker got the daemon to treat that identity as trusted. During an automatic repair, the daemon re-encrypted the top-level keys to the attacker's key. The demo needed no root, no user password and no prompts. It recovered saved passwords, Wi-Fi credentials and stored cards. Matter home keys also unlocked a smart lock, and passkey-protected logins could be replayed. A second bug let iCloud backups hold an escrow secret protected only by a device-bound key, so a wiped phone could still yield data.

Apple patched both issues under CVE-2026-28860, and the presenters withheld proof-of-concept code. Their takeaways are to watch the trusted peers database for unexpected writes, since legitimate changes are rare, and to avoid reusing passwords across accounts. They also described an undocumented CloudKit reset command for compromised accounts, with a warning that it can cause data loss.

talks.title: Install Me Maybe - Turning Claimable VS Code Extension IDs into Supply Chain Attacks
talks.teaser: Shows how VS Code extension identifiers can be claimed on a second marketplace to run code on developer machines, and what measured callbacks revealed.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how editor extensions are identified and trusted. A VS Code extension is named publisher.extension, but the publisher namespace belongs to one marketplace. The Visual Studio Marketplace and Open VSX are separate registries, and forks such as Cursor and Windsurf inherit VS Code's extension recommendations and settings imports. An identifier trusted on one marketplace can therefore be unclaimed on the other. The speaker calls this extension confusion and frames it as a mix of dependency confusion and name takeover: claim the missing namespace, publish under the same identifier, and any machine that resolves it runs your code.

The research started with extensions.json and devcontainer.json recommendations, then moved to a direct comparison of the two catalogs. Thousands of popular extensions had unclaimed publishers on Open VSX, which the speaker estimated reached hundreds of millions of installs. He published research extensions in three waves. They reported only basic attribution data such as hostname, IP, editor, install path, and a corporate email domain and Git remote, all disclosed in each readme. Across about four months they produced roughly 1.5 million callbacks from more than 160 countries and around 300 disclosures, with some bounties paid.

The practical takeaways are to use an allow list for each marketplace, block unapproved installs, disable automatic extension updates where possible, add a cool-down period for newly published extensions, and review bootstrap scripts and dev containers for stale identifiers. The speaker reports that the marketplace has agreed to add protections against claiming namespaces one does not control, but at the time of the talk they were not yet deployed.

talks.title: Identity Crisis - Novel Vulnerabilities leading to Kerberos Downgrade, DoS, and Full Domain Takeover
talks.teaser: Shows how invisible Unicode characters defeat uniqueness checks on Active Directory SPNs and UPNs, enabling Kerberos downgrade, denial of service and domain takeover.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a persistence technique that uses invisible Unicode characters to create Active Directory accounts that look like duplicates. The speaker found that the directory ignores some of these characters in LDAP filters, so a query without the character still returns the object. That behavior led to a question about whether uniqueness checks on other attributes could be sidestepped in the same way.

Service principal names and user principal names must be unique across the forest, but the speaker showed that the check can be bypassed with unfilterable characters. A duplicate host-class SPN lets an attacker deny service to a share, and an explicit duplicate makes the domain controller fail Kerberos so clients silently fall back to NTLM. A second chain abuses the Kerberos change-password flow. A low-privileged user spoofs a UPN that matches a domain admin's account name, obtains a ticket that the domain controller accepts, and resets the admin's password. The speaker reported both issues to Microsoft, which patched them in March and April.

For defenders, the recommendation is to patch domain controllers first. If patching is delayed, the talk suggests alerting on SPN or UPN changes that collide with existing values, and correlating them with password reset events. The speaker also stressed least privilege, MFA and behavioral detection for tier-zero accounts. A tool that automates the attack flow was announced for testing.

talks.title: How much of our Bluetooth firmware reverse engineering work can now be automated with LLMs
talks.teaser: Shows how LLM agents driving Ghidra can map Bluetooth controller firmware to spec-required HCI and link-layer code paths, using reusable skills and ground-truth grading.
talks.summary:
The speakers had reverse engineered Realtek, Texas Instruments and Silicon Labs Bluetooth chip firmware by hand, and wanted to know how much of that work a large language model could take over. Local models were too weak on obscure Bluetooth facts, so they tested frontier models. They connected Claude Code to Ghidra through an MCP server that can run arbitrary Ghidra scripts, then packaged their prompts as a skill that locates spec-mandated code such as HCI command handlers, LMP and LLCP packet senders and receivers, and the structures the spec defines.

The main technique is what they call waypoints: code the specification requires must exist somewhere in the firmware, so prompts can point the model at it. Prompts are ordered by dependency and parallelized where possible. A self-improving loop failed to converge, so they instead tuned each category separately and stopped once it reached the known functions. Evaluation used five firmware images with known symbols, then seven unseen ones graded by two models cross-checking each other. Chips lacking Classic support or a separate HCI layer produced far fewer findings, because those layers were absent. A full run took roughly five and a half to eight and a half hours.

The practical takeaway is that a firmware analyst can save days of renaming and structure work by writing spec-derived prompts, validating them against binaries with known answers, and running results through more than one model. The authors suggest the same approach would suit other spec-driven firmware such as Wi-Fi, USB, NVMe or UEFI. The skills were released publicly.

talks.title: High Voltage Heist - Turning Your EV into my Power Bank
talks.teaser: Shows how a parked EV's charging handshake can be spoofed so its traction battery powers an outside device, and introduces the ChargeSploit test toolkit.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with how an electric vehicle and its charger communicate during DC charging. The speakers, from an embedded security testing team, walk through the control pilot signalling, the power line communication sounding step that pairs a car with its charger, and the network discovery that follows. They then cover the ISO 15118 and older DIN session sequence, from protocol negotiation and pre-charge through current demand loops to welding detection at the end. They note that the network management key is sent in plaintext early in the exchange, so it adds little protection against a man-in-the-middle.

The core question was whether the vehicle's battery management system believes what the charger reports. To test this, the team built ChargeSploit, a software and hardware toolkit that can simulate a vehicle or charger, sit in the middle of a live session, and manipulate control pilot and proximity pilot signals. Their rig also included a programmable load and an adjustable high-voltage supply for the DC pins. Against a Tesla Model 3, the car measured voltage only during pre-charge and then accepted false voltage and current figures. With a bank of kettles giving roughly 12 to 15 kilowatts of load, the team drained the traction battery, and a phone was charged from a locked car in the demo.

For practitioners, the takeaway is that the vehicle trusts charger-supplied values once the session is running. The speakers described possible harm beyond unauthorized power: permanent battery damage if discharge goes far below normal limits, and denial of service through a short circuit on the pins. They released a restricted version of the tooling and stressed that the voltages involved are lethal.

talks.title: Hacking Your Life with AI Can Get You Hacked - How AI Orchestration Platforms Ship RCE by Design
talks.teaser: Shows how AI orchestration platforms such as Langflow, Flowise and Airflow ship remote code execution through prompt injection and trust boundary failures.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a model of AI orchestration platforms. A workflow starts at a trigger such as a webhook, schedule or inbound message, passes through an LLM step, then reaches code nodes that run Python or JavaScript before producing an output. The speaker argues that these products assume anyone who can edit a workflow is trusted to run code on the host.

Across seven platforms, the speaker reports multiple CVEs and critical findings, grouped into recurring patterns. These include string-based filters that are easy to bypass, a sandbox hardening call that was commented out, eval and exec applied to LLM output, and a sandbox bootstrap ordered after the code it was meant to contain. Some endpoints needed no authentication at all. One demo chained a single prompt injection into an LLM module to reach remote code execution without logging in.

Vendor responses ranged from fixes to calling code execution intended behavior, with one project's own documentation teaching the vulnerable pattern. The talk closes with a five-step method for auditing these platforms: map inputs, trace sinks, check execution order, test reachability by low-privilege callers, and check the docs. Defenders are advised to require authentication on execution paths, disable dangerous flags, and assume persistent compromise.

talks.title: Hacking the Hackers who Hack Hackers - Supply Chain Backdoors in Underground VPN Infrastructure
talks.teaser: Traces how the FirewallFalcon VPN and SSH management toolkit was weaponized to backdoor its own operators and enable man-in-the-middle interception.
talks.summary:
