The talk starts with underground VPN resale operations that advertise cheap or free access through Telegram, and with FirewallFalcon Manager, an open-source server management tool promoted in those channels. The speaker, who runs a honeypot network, noticed the tool's install traffic and its community links, then looked at the operator's activity and at the reseller product built on top of it.

Behind the installer, the research found an SSH configuration exposed to the internet with root access, a secret in a companion project, and a proxy binary that added a rogue root certificate and a hosts-file entry so traffic could be decrypted in transit. Git history of the repository showed an earlier version with a layered install script that hid an encrypted binary and reported the host's details to an attacker-run Telegram bot. That version also created a backdoor user. A DNS component embedded a privileged key, which allowed querying records for roughly 650 installed machines across several regions. Many of those hosts looked compromised, with open ports, misconfigurations, and certificates belonging to unrelated organizations.

The takeaway is that people who deploy hacker tooling can be targeted by that tooling. Operators of rented or stolen servers should treat such scripts as hostile, check certificates and DNS on their hosts, and review repository history and binaries before trusting them. The speaker noted that the project later moved to another code host and that the operation's current status was unclear at the time of the talk.

talks.title: Hacking the EOD Bot How I Learned to Love the Boomba
talks.teaser: Teardown of a surplus PackBot bomb disposal robot, exposing unencrypted radios, plaintext control links, and a command injection flaw in its tablet app.
talks.summary:
The speakers bought a surplus PackBot, a bomb disposal robot built on early 2000s engineering, and took it apart to see how it works. They start with its history, from a DARPA-funded design through several corporate owners, and walk through the hardware: a Linux single-board computer, a stack of five circuit layers, standardized accessory ports that carry 24 volts on some pins, and a rear maintenance port they mapped with a custom cable.

The software half covers how the robot is controlled. Operators log in over SSH with a shared default password, all processes run as root, and sessions are created over plain HTTP, so someone on the same network can release another operator's session. Video runs as multicast UDP. The team decoded the JAUS command protocol from the tablet app's APK to build a Wireshark dissector, and they found that the 4.9 GHz mesh radio's OpenVPN overlay was unencrypted. They replaced that radio with custom hardware and ran the tablet app on newer Android versions and a Steam Deck.

The closing section argues that a walled-garden perimeter is not enough and that protocols need protection too. Recommended steps include secure boot, dm-verity and encrypted filesystems, and retiring legacy platforms before technical debt piles up. The speakers also note that obscurity only delays analysis, and that coordinated disclosure with the vendor went smoothly.

talks.title: Hacking Jetskis - from Sea-Don't to Sea-Doo
talks.teaser: Reverse-engineers a Sea-Doo jetski's diagnostic protocol and one-wire key interface to build an open-source, programmable replacement key.
talks.summary:
A friend bought a 2000 Sea-Doo jetski without its key, and the official dealer tooling cost more than the machine itself. With no public documentation, the speaker began by reverse-engineering the diagnostic software's CAN protocol, which uses KWP2000 with authenticated security levels. Checking the adapter path, the speaker wrote a compatible adapter DLL for cheap CAN hardware. The bus turned out not to be the route for this model, though. The real programming access is a one-wire interface on the key post, handled by a separate electronic module.

Logic analysis of the key handshake showed a one-wire token protocol. The speaker found firmware for the programmer inside the software bundle, which targets a Motorola HC08 microcontroller. A download command in the adapter firmware dumped the module's EEPROM without writing anything, and a checksum brute force over the dump located the key IDs. The data also exposed the VIN, engine hours and the number of enrolled keys. Using this, the team built a key that got the engine running on the bench, and later a Flipper Zero app that reads the module and emulates saved keys.

For a portable solution, the speaker designed a small ATtiny circuit that charges capacitors from the one-wire signal alone, with cycle-precise handwritten assembly. It was mounted on a small PCB in a printed enclosure. The main takeaway is how a proprietary immobilizer can be understood from its wire-level behavior, and how a cheap programmable replacement becomes possible without the paid tools.

talks.title: gpwn Wiretapping fiber GPON ISP deployments from the comfort of your home
talks.teaser: Demonstrates how a roughly $100 rig can eavesdrop on neighbors over shared GPON fiber, then take over the provider's line terminal from the subscriber side.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a fiber installation the speakers followed step by step, then asks where a household gets separated from its neighbors when the street splitter is purely passive. It explains GPON, the fiber-to-home standard whose downstream broadcast relies on optional encryption that many vendors ship switched off. Basic terminology is covered: the line terminal at the provider, the subscriber unit at each home, and the passive tree linking them.

Using a consumer subscriber unit built on a Realtek chipset, the researchers bypassed several filtering layers to capture downstream frames from neighbors. The captures showed unencrypted DNS, POP3, SIP and RTP, along with GTP-tunneled 4G and 5G backhaul from nearby towers. They also showed that unsecured street splitters allow upstream capture. On the provider side, they fuzzed the provisioning handshake on a white-label line terminal, found that injected HTML rendered in an administrator's discovery page, and chained it to a command injection that yielded root.

Control of the terminal exposes subscriber encryption keys, lawful-intercept features, and firmware pushes to every connected unit, which can reach customer routers. Recommendations cover locking splitters, enabling downstream encryption, patching line terminal firmware, and not relying on the ISP for privacy. The team released a tool for scanning gem ports and recording traffic, and said the vendor only partly fixed the flaw after about 90 days.

talks.title: Gotta Catch 'Em All - How To Capture 3.5 Billion WhatsApp Accounts
talks.teaser: Shows how predictable phone-number identifiers and weak rate limits let one machine enumerate billions of WhatsApp accounts and their public metadata.
talks.summary:
Contact discovery in messengers usually means checking phone numbers against a service's user base. That becomes an enumeration problem when identifiers are predictable and server-side limits are loose. The speakers tested whether WhatsApp still allowed this at scale. Using an open-source reimplementation of the WhatsApp web protocol, they sent well-formed lookups from one IP address and a few test accounts. They began with a public scrape of about 500 million numbers, and more than half were still active years after the leak.

They then generated candidate numbers from national numbering plans, covering 235 countries and about 63 billion candidates. The run took roughly three weeks and found around 3.5 billion active accounts without any bans. Each hit also yielded profile photos, about text, public keys and device details. The team reported that 57 percent of accounts had public photos, that some encryption keys were reused across many accounts in regions tied to scam operations, and that about-text fields exposed drug sales and other sensitive content. They also observed activity in countries where the app is restricted.

Earlier disclosure tickets about missing rate limits were closed as duplicates or non-issues until a public paper prompted engagement. Meta then rolled out countermeasures starting in October 2025, including rate limiting and removal of some timestamps. The takeaways: metadata leaks even when messages are end-to-end encrypted, leaked data stays useful for years, and centralized messengers concentrate risk.

talks.title: Gone in 60 Frames - USB Video Exploitation
talks.teaser: Walks through turning a Linux USB Video class out-of-bounds write and an HID info leak into a reliable root shell from a plugged-in device.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a 2025 Amnesty International and Google TAG report on an in-the-wild chain of Linux kernel USB bugs used against phones. That report described the vulnerabilities but not how to exploit them. The speakers, from NCC Group, set out to close that gap. They mapped the USB attack surface, noting that desktop distributions enable far more device classes than a typical Android kernel, and explained descriptor hierarchies and class specifications such as HID, UVC and mass storage. They also described their experience building tooling to insert and remove emulated USB devices programmatically.

The middle section covers two bugs. The first is an information disclosure in the HID raw request path, where a malformed buffer makes a length underflow to a very large value, leaking about 64 KB of kernel memory. The team matched recurring kernel text pointers against known offsets to recover the kernel base, bypassing KASLR. The second is an out-of-bounds write in the UVC driver, triggered by a specific quirk. The speakers turned a min/max check into a way to locate a writable 32-bit value near the frame interval pointer, then used it to overwrite the uevent_helper path so that a script on an attacker-supplied USB stick runs as root.

The talk closes with a live demonstration on an Ubuntu desktop. A single emulated USB device leaks the kernel base, performs the write and returns a root reverse shell. The takeaway is that USB is a practical attack vector, and that inexpensive hardware and a small amount of custom tooling are enough to build a working exploit. The speakers point listeners to the full written paper for the details they could not cover.

talks.title: Going the Distance - Long Range Keystroke Injection via LoRa Mesh Networks
talks.teaser: Shows how a keystroke-injection implant planted on a USB port can be triggered remotely over a LoRa Meshtastic mesh, without internet or Wi-Fi.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a building-infiltration scenario: an attacker gets brief physical access, plants a device, and needs a way to trigger it later. The speaker reviews the limits of existing USB keystroke-injection tools. Prerecorded payloads are fire-and-forget, and their Wi-Fi command channels are useless on air-gapped networks. The proposed alternative is a device that receives text commands over long-range LoRa radio and relays them through the Meshtastic mesh, so no internet or Wi-Fi is needed.

The middle of the talk covers the build. The project, M.I.A., re-implements the Meshtastic protocol on a radio library instead of the stock firmware. Most of the difficulty was getting LoRa radio parameters exactly right, decoding protobuf field structure, and fixing AES counter-mode nonce handling. The speaker also noted a key-size discrepancy on the default channel. Commands use a text prefix that the device parses into keystrokes. A live demo sent a command from a stock node that made the target machine open a website.

The speaker closes by listing limits: physical access is still required, range depends heavily on obstacles, and mesh traffic is hard to detect. For defenders, the suggestions were controlling which USB devices may connect and scanning for unexpected radio activity with software-defined radios. The firmware, hardware design and tooling are promised as open source.

talks.title: From Wind Farm to CHP Plant - Private APN Lateral Movement in a Polish Energy Sector Attack
talks.teaser: Traces a Polish combined heat and power plant intrusion to a forgotten cellular router and a private APN that linked it to wind farm networks.
talks.summary:
The talk covers a second, smaller combined heat and power plant hit in the same late-December 2025 campaign against Polish energy operators. The plant's operator first called the problems a controller fault, and the investigation stalled on dead ends: a remote access device that had been offline since before the attack, an unknown second remote access device found on the network, and a controller whose storage was wiped before the team could image it.

The breakthrough came from treating the cellular connectivity as a hypothesis to test. The team traced the plant's controllers to SIM-based cellular routers on a private APN shared with the grid operator. Only after pressing the operator to check the correct SIM did logs show suspicious VNC attempts and scanning. A router pulled from a frozen wind farm roof held logs even after a factory reset, and its SSH sessions lined up with the plant's destructive actions. The intruder had pivoted from a compromised firewall at the wind farm, through the router's management interface, into the APN, then reached a controller with default credentials and enabled SSH on it. Siemens PLCs were stopped and reset, Moxa devices were reconfigured, and the steam turbine shut down, but consumers saw no impact.

For practitioners, the lessons are that a private APN should not be treated as trusted when the operator does not control its configuration, that client isolation was missing so every site could reach every other, and that cellular router management interfaces need the same restrictions as serial links. The talk also argues that persistence matters: slow ISP and vendor log delivery nearly ended the investigation before the right device was found.

talks.title: From square root to root - escalating privileges in Azure containers with Python in Excel
talks.teaser: Shows how a symlink flaw in the file upload path of Microsoft's Python in Excel containers led to root, and how Excel's trust prompts were bypassed.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a practical question: Excel's Python feature sends user code to a cloud container, so could that code reach Microsoft-owned servers? The researchers begin with basic reconnaissance from a low-privilege account, then map the helper services around the container and reverse-engineer the API the Excel client uses to submit code.

The central finding is in the file upload flow. The service writes uploaded data as root into paths whose names the client can predict and partly control. By placing a symbolic link at the location used for the ETAG output and hiding a payload in the ETAG value, they overwrote a setuid-related binary that a root-level service runs on a schedule, which gave them root. From there they recovered service binaries and a deployment configuration file that exposed internal component names and architecture, reached container hosts across many regions, and found that some images were publicly pullable, including pilot builds. Microsoft responded by checking for symbolic links in file operations.

On the Excel side, the researchers observed that Python workbooks skip the trusted-records prompt that macros trigger. A returned web image object could make the client fetch an arbitrary URL, which could be used to move data back into the isolated container. This led to CVE-2026-45459, covering both the trusted records warning and network isolation. The practical takeaways are to enforce least privilege on anything a service writes as root, and to keep deployment details and skill files off production hosts.

talks.title: LaunchBreak a Sip of Tea, a Click, and a Full Multi stage Desktop Takeover
talks.teaser: Shows how a single crafted browser link can launch Electron desktop apps and chain them across processes into full remote code execution.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the spread of custom URI schemes in AI and agentic desktop apps, which let a browser link install plugins or MCP servers and import configuration in one click. Earlier Electron research assumed an attacker already controlled the renderer. This work instead models an attacker who begins outside the app, with only a link, and follows the input through the main, utility and renderer processes until it reaches a dangerous sink.

The researchers organize these bugs along three axes: where the payload comes from (the URI itself, a second payload fetched from an attacker server during processing, or a file dropped to disk and loaded later), how it moves across processes over IPC, and which sinks it reaches, such as command execution, dynamic evaluation or module loading. To find such chains they built Proton, a fuzzing framework that uses an LLM to map taint flows and then fuzzes each segment separately before composing them. Across 589 applications they report 18 zero-days, 17 of them remote code execution, with 11 CVEs assigned and a bounty from Vercel.

The "tea time" section walks through several cases: a terminal app that concatenated URL fields into a shell command, a mail client whose unsanitized HTML was reachable through a file-protocol origin quirk, an EPUB reader where disabled context isolation allowed prototype pollution to reach privileged objects, and a local server with path traversal. For users, the takeaway is to avoid trusting external links and to be careful with always-allow prompts. For developers, the key lessons are to keep untrusted input away from shell and eval sinks and to enable context isolation.

talks.title: Plug And Pwn Weaponizing Windows PnP Auto Install
talks.teaser: Shows how a USB device, or one forged over RDP, can make Windows Plug and Play run vendor installer code as SYSTEM, using chained low-severity flaws.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how Windows Plug and Play can silently fetch a signed vendor driver package when a USB device appears and run its installer code as SYSTEM, without administrator rights. The presenters, from Accenture's offensive security team, opened with a live demo on a fresh Windows 11 machine. They then chained two low-severity flaws from separate vendors: a named pipe exposed by a modem service that let them change the machine's DNS, and a co-installer that trusted configuration files fetched over plain HTTP and allowed path traversal into System32. Hardware was emulated with FaceDancer rather than real devices.

The second part moved the same install path onto RDP USB redirection. The server builds a device from descriptors the client sends, and a group policy setting decides whether that device is accepted. Where that gate was open, a forged camera identity sent by a standard user session triggered a DLL hijack in a signed camera package, giving SYSTEM code execution with no physical access. The team also described PnP Simulate, a tool for comparing Windows Update discovery with the real installation flow, and noted that many matches never reached automatic installation. Further stages used a vendor service with a hard-coded check and a registry-writing admin service.

The takeaways were that a valid signature says little about whether every service and installer was reviewed from an attacker's viewpoint, and that low-severity bugs can combine into serious impact. Mitigations mentioned included blocking unneeded USB device classes, disabling RDP USB redirection where it is not needed, and keeping drivers updated. The presenters said proof-of-concept code and tooling would be published.

talks.title: No Socket, No Privs, No Problem - Weaponizing OCI Registries
talks.teaser: Shows how pulling artifacts from malicious OCI registries can become SSRF, file reads, and container escape in tools like Ollama and Docker Model Runner.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether a routine container or model pull, which needs no special privileges, can be turned into an attack. The presenters briefly explain OCI registries: manifests describe blobs named by SHA-256 digest, and clients talk a JSON-over-HTTP distribution protocol. They focus on Ollama and Docker Model Runner because both give registry client access to users who do not have host access.

The middle covers the findings. A malicious registry can answer an authentication challenge with an arbitrary URL, so the client makes server-side requests to internal services or cloud metadata endpoints. Depending on the response, the client either forwards a token to the attacker or returns the full response to the caller, which makes a read-capable SSRF. In Ollama, exposed servers without authentication could be made to copy host files through crafted manifest paths, and because no hash verification happened, SSH keys, environment variables, and cloud credentials could be exfiltrated. On macOS, Docker Model Runner's inference libraries run as host processes, and a model definition file executed on load gave code execution outside the sandbox.

The closing section covers vendor responses. Some reports went unanswered for more than 90 days, some earned CVEs, and Apple judged one issue to be working as intended. The speakers said roughly 75,000 Ollama servers were still internet-exposed when they rechecked. The takeaway is that any tool using OCI in some form may offer similar primitives, so pulls from untrusted registries should be treated as untrusted input.

talks.title: Need Better Password Cracking - Throw Out the Alphabet
talks.teaser: Shows how a Markov password generator that models GPT-2 subword tokens instead of characters outguesses OMEN and Hashcat masks on leaked and enterprise-style passwords.
talks.summary:
Gorenflo starts from the limits of character-based password guessing. Hashcat masks, wordlists, and rules work well until a password breaks the expected pattern, such as several capitalized words in a passphrase, and then attackers fall back to brute force. He argues that people type passwords in predictable chunks, so the unit being modeled matters more than the model itself.

His tool, tokenov, trains a trigram Markov model on RockYou, but splits passwords into tokens from GPT-2's tokenizer instead of single characters. The talk benchmarks it against John the Ripper, Hashcat, OMEN, and PCFG at fixed candidate budgets. Early CPU-only runs favored tokenov, but he admits the comparison undersold Hashcat's GPU throughput. Under time-boxed tests with best66 and enterprise-style filters (8+ characters, three of four character classes), tokenov came out ahead. He also notes that a much smaller tokenizer trained on password data may work better than the general-purpose one.

He closes with the practical side: a bootstrap command, generation piped into Hashcat, password scoring by rarity bits, seeding from OSINT wordlists, checkpoint resume, and model files that bundle their tokenizer. His takeaway is that character count stops being a reliable strength measure when a long password reduces to a few tokens. Rules help in most cases, except with very slow hashes. The tool is young research, and he invites others to build their own models.

talks.title: OffGuard - Breaking the Most Popular AI Gateway from Auth Bypass to Cloud Compromise
talks.teaser: Walks through three LiteLLM flaws, an MCP authentication bypass, a guardrail sandbox escape, and an SSRF path to cloud credentials, plus internet-scale exposure data.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with LiteLLM, an open-source AI gateway that holds provider API keys, routes prompts and responses, and connects to tools over MCP. The speaker began by mapping internet-exposed instances and found that roughly one in ten either accepted the default master key or required no authentication at all. That master key also grants admin login and can sign session JWTs, so knowing it exposes much of the deployment.

The middle of the talk covers three attack paths. A guardrail registration endpoint skipped the forbidden-pattern checks and built-in stripping that the test endpoint applied, so custom code ran with root privileges in the container. A pass-through proxy did not validate target URLs, which allowed SSRF to the cloud metadata service. Because the proxy let callers set arbitrary headers, the attacker could complete the IMDSv2 token handshake and retrieve role credentials. A separate MCP authentication handler returned an unrestricted session whenever any Authorization header was present, letting an unauthenticated caller list and execute connected tools. The speaker also reported honeypot captures in which an attacker chained the MCP bypass with another flaw to deploy a crypto miner. The RCE and MCP issues were patched in earlier releases.

The closing advice is to treat AI gateways as high-value infrastructure, rotate default keys, disable MCP when it is not needed, and keep these services off reachable networks even internally. The speaker also argues that teams deploying gateways often skip the review applied to other application endpoints.

talks.title: Lessons from a decade of building whistleblower tech
talks.teaser: Traces a decade of building SecureDrop, the open-source whistleblower submission system, and previews WEBCAT, a browser code-verification project.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the 2012 episode in which a source struggled to reach a journalist over PGP, a story that led to the Snowden disclosures. It then describes the wider problem: journalists lost their legal shield as governments obtained metadata from tech companies, and sources are often exposed by who they contacted rather than by what they said. SecureDrop grew from Aaron Swartz's unfinished prototype into a platform now used by dozens of major news outlets.

The middle of the talk covers the design lessons the team learned. Newsrooms self-host the system on their own servers, and sources connect through Tor onion services. Because sources often need long conversations, the system uses random passphrases instead of accounts with recovery. Spam and malware are handled by moving document review from a manual air-gapped workflow into Qubes, where each file is opened in a disposable, isolated virtual machine. The speakers explain why end-to-end encryption in a web browser is hard, since a compromised server can serve malicious code, and they describe a protocol designed with ETH Zurich researchers.

The talk closes with WEBCAT, a manifest-and-transparency approach to verifying web code before it runs. It is currently a browser extension and is being bundled into Tor Browser. The takeaway for practitioners is to model the threat carefully, and to treat browser code integrity as a real gap for any anonymous or end-to-end encrypted web tool.

talks.title: Looking and Peering - Attacking from beyond BGP Adjacency
talks.teaser: Shows how an outsider can reach BGP routers that are not direct peers, using looking glass command injection, VPN tunnel injection, and malformed-attribute parser bugs.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a common assumption: a BGP router only accepts updates from configured peers, and GTSM's TTL check confirms that the peer is one hop away. The speaker argues that this adjacency boundary is the weak point, since most hardening work such as RPKI and BGPsec focuses on route validation. The question is whether an attacker without a peering session can get inside that boundary.

The attack path has three stages. First, looking glass web tools that pass user input into a router shell can give command execution on an edge router, and the speaker reports that several such tools are still vulnerable. Second, tunnel injection through a misconfigured VPN endpoint lets an off-path attacker appear adjacent to a target, and a use-after-free in FRR's attribute caching leads to remote code execution. Third, differences between FRR, BIRD and other daemons are abused: oversized or malformed optional attributes, and mismatched prefix limits, make one implementation re-emit or reject updates in a way that causes repeated session resets in another. A recorded demo shows a victim session dropping after the chain runs.

The speaker estimates exposure from PeeringDB data, counting roughly 300 networks running vulnerable looking glass software. The reach is still small compared with the total number of networks, and large default-free routers complicate any wide outage. The practical takeaways are to treat looking glasses as privileged systems, validate attribute lengths strictly, and avoid assuming that a peer list alone protects a router.

talks.title: Rage Against the Sandbox - Bypassing - iOS Sec - to Run Unsigned Code w SSH
talks.teaser: Shows how to run an SSH server, interactive shells and unsigned binaries on a jailed iPhone by reimplementing fork() and code-signing checks in user space.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a practical problem. On a stock iPhone, the sandbox blocks fork() and code signing blocks unsigned code, so researchers who want a shell with job control are left with full-system emulation or the hunt for scarce jailbreak bugs. The speaker sets out to get around both limits without exploiting a vulnerability, using only standard APIs.

The approach rebuilds what a POSIX shell depends on inside an ordinary app. Each virtual process is a group of threads with its own file descriptor and signal tables. The fork replacement duplicates a per-process heap and the writable data of loaded libraries, rewrites stale pointers, and copies stack frames onto a new thread, using setjmp and longjmp to hop onto a temporary stack. A custom linker loads unsigned binaries without executable permissions, and an emulator runs them, with calls into signed code handed back to the host CPU.

The demo connects over SSH to a phone running the app, opens a shell where ifconfig and vim work, and then runs a public kernel race exploit delivered as an unsigned binary, which gains access to a folder that was previously blocked. The main takeaway is that the platform's process and signing checks can be reproduced in user space, at a real speed cost, since the naive fork took seconds.

talks.title: Patch Gap to Mobile Renderer RCE - Pwning Samsung Internets V8
talks.teaser: Shows how an outdated V8 engine in Samsung Internet on the Galaxy S25 turns a known Ignition bug into renderer code execution and universal XSS.
talks.summary:
Samsung Internet on the Galaxy S25 shipped with a V8 build from May 2025 that already had public, fixed bugs, and the proper fix did not land until months later. The speakers explain why an outdated embedded JavaScript engine is an attractive n-day target, then analyze CVE-2025-10891: an integer truncation in Ignition's exception handler table that redirects control flow to an unintended bytecode offset.

The exploit relies on bytecode smuggling. Constants loaded into the instruction stream are reinterpreted as opcodes once execution jumps into them, and repeated arithmetic that advances feedback slots lets the author place larger payloads in that stream. The chain calls a privileged runtime function to deserialize a WebAssembly module whose optimized machine code is replaced with attacker-chosen instructions, giving code execution in the renderer. The attack was developed on x86 and ported to ARM for the phone.

The second stage addresses the renderer's limits. Phones only isolate sites where the user logs in, so a patched renderer can be reused for a logged-in service such as Gmail. The authors hook the built-in construct function with a callback that calls a debug evaluation routine, which runs JavaScript without the CSP check, yielding universal XSS. A live demo redirected a victim to Gmail and read the inbox. The takeaway is to keep embedded engines current and not to assume mobile isolation contains a compromised renderer.

talks.title: One Chain to Own Them All - Breaking AI Infrastructures
talks.teaser: Shows how a PyTorch deserialization flaw, reached through AI inference APIs, turns a local model-loading bug into remote code execution.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with the growing use of AI tooling and the infrastructure behind it: vector stores, model inference servers and GPU container runtimes. The presenters explain why these components became targets, pointing to recent competitions that featured Ollama, Triton and vLLM. Their search focused on vLLM's completions endpoint, which accepts prompt embeddings, decodes them and passes them to torch.load. They had earlier found a bypass of PyTorch's weights_only mode, and they asked whether the same class of bug could return after the fix.

The middle of the talk walks through a new heap out-of-bounds flaw in the unpickler's tensor rebuild path, which lets a crafted model file declare more elements than its storage holds. The team turned the over-read into an information leak using an error-based technique, then used an out-of-bounds write to overwrite a tensor destructor pointer. On some default Python builds without position-independent executables, the address of the system function was predictable, which removed the need for a separate leak. The same pattern appeared in other products, including ComfyUI, SGLang, NVIDIA Dynamo and OpenLM, where model loading, LoRA or image-embedding inputs reach torch.load.

The main takeaway is that any API that loads models or tensors from user-supplied input is a deserialization surface, even when the model is described as remote rather than local. Teams should not treat weights_only as a complete safety boundary, should audit where torch.load is reachable, and should keep inference servers on patched versions and off unnecessary optional features.

talks.title: No Prompt Required - Pre Task RCE in Google Gemini CLI
talks.teaser: Shows how a project config file loaded before Gemini CLI's sandbox starts gave attackers host code execution in CI, and how to audit similar pre-task inputs.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at AI agent security from a point before the prompt. The speaker argues that agents read project configuration, environment files, and startup parameters before the model handles any task. In headless CI runs no person is present to approve actions, and the workspace is treated as trusted, so the decisions made at load time carry the most weight. Prompt injection and guardrails do not cover this path.

The main case is Google's Gemini CLI, run as a GitHub action to review pull requests. The speaker walked through its three defenses: a container sandbox, environment sanitization that strips secrets, and a tool allow-list. Each of these runs after a project-level environment file has already been loaded in trusted mode. A proxy setting for the sandbox was then passed to a shell with shell enabled, which allowed command injection on the host. A demonstration showed a fork pull request reaching code execution on the runner host. Google rated the issue CVSS 10.0, patched it, and changed how it handles workspace trust. The speaker also cited a similar pre-trust configuration issue in Claude Code and a changed trust prompt in OpenAI Codex.

The closing guidance is a simple audit method for any agent. First, list every input the system accepts before work starts, including config files, startup flags, and protocol handshakes. Second, record what authority each input carries. Third, check whether that authority can reach command execution or change policy. If it can, the speaker says defenses applied at prompt time will not help.

talks.title: MSIX'd Up - Weaponizing the Modern Windows App Packaging Ecosystem
talks.teaser: Shows how Windows app packaging features like MSIX, AppContainers and package capabilities can be abused for initial access, lateral movement and SYSTEM privilege escalation.
talks.summary:
Nick Powers argues that the Windows app packaging stack, which includes MSIX, AppContainers, package identity and capabilities, is widely deployed yet rarely studied from an offensive angle. He walks through an attack path in stages, starting with initial access. The MS App Installer protocol handler has been disabled, but app installer files can still stage a signed MSIX install that streams the package into memory. Scraping about 40,000 Store apps showed that nearly half declared the restricted run-full-trust capability, so publishing a capable app proved easier than he expected.

Once on a host, he shows that AppContainer processes can be launched with capabilities such as internet client, broad file system access and enterprise authentication. Some standard file APIs were denied, but a Win32 wrapper path honored the capability. He demonstrates this with a Mythic agent and notes that the EDR products he reviewed did not inject user-mode hooks into these processes, though kernel telemetry still sees them. For lateral movement, he installs a certificate and pushes a package through WMI MDM classes, then activates it over DCOM from a WMI event subscription so it applies to all users.

For privilege escalation, a logic flaw in the modifiable apps capability, combined with symbolic links, yields an arbitrary read. Pairing that with an MSI installed at a UI level that does not require admin lets the attacker create a volume shadow copy and read the SAM, SYSTEM and SECURITY hives. The main prerequisite is that system protection is enabled. He closes with defensive ideas, such as hunting for AppContainer processes with no matching installed package and for packages installed from remote URIs.

talks.title: Lowering the Orbit - Exploiting Proprietary Satellite Protocols via Software Defined Radio and GS
talks.teaser: Shows how an open-source, deliberately vulnerable CubeSat platform lets researchers practice radio attacks on CCSDS space packets.
talks.summary:
Romel Marin opens with the gap that motivated the project. Space protocol documentation is easy to find, but there is no legal satellite to practice radio attacks against, and the number of active spacecraft keeps growing. He covers the basics a newcomer needs: a satellite as a computer in orbit, telemetry, telecommands and payload data, the link between space and ground segments, and the CCSDS standards with the Space Packet Protocol structure.

The core of the talk is PWNSAT, an open-source platform of intentionally vulnerable hardware. He describes its three versions, ending with a CubeSat built from a flight computer that runs Linux, a LoRa radio board and a power board, plus a plug-and-play ground station application. The demonstrations use a cheap RTL-SDR receiver to capture unencrypted downlink traffic and decode the packets. He then brute-forces application process identifiers over the Space Packet Protocol, much as directory scanning works against web applications, injects captured data back into the link, and fuzzes the firmware to trigger a denial of service.

The takeaway is that the downlink in these demos carries no cryptography, so anyone designing or assessing a space link should treat the radio path as an attack surface. He publishes the scripts, firmware, PCB designs and step-by-step walkthroughs on GitHub, along with about 34 documented vulnerabilities. He stresses that the tools are meant for lab hardware like his, not for real spacecraft.

talks.title: Lights Out - Out of Band, Out of Mind, Out of Control
talks.teaser: Shows how baseboard management controllers leak credentials over IPMI and how an attacker can pivot from them into the host server they manage.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at baseboard management controllers, the always-on secondary computers built into enterprise servers. These devices run their own operating system and network stack, often share a network port with the host, and have been poorly secured since IPMI was criticized in 2013. The speaker explains how they end up exposed, both on the internet and on corporate networks.

The research team scanned about 15,000 internet-facing and 125,000 internal devices. They found that many systems returned RAKP password hashes without any credentials, and they cracked thousands of them offline. The talk walks through a chain of authentication flaws: handshake state confusion, session privilege relabeling, skipped integrity and encryption checks, a default key in OpenBMC, and a KVM token derived from the clock. Vendor-specific problems are covered too, including a hardcoded Supermicro password and a Dell attempt to block IPMI that only applied to IPv4. Once a controller is compromised, the speaker shows how its access to host memory over internal buses and DMA can reach the host, and how the factory password scheme made default passwords easier to crack.

The main takeaways are to disable the host-side KCS interface, keep the management NIC on a dedicated network, and treat BMC firmware as part of the trust boundary. The speaker released OOBscan, an open-source IPMI exploitation tool, along with a John the Ripper patch for the new hash format, and noted that most issues remain unpatched.

talks.title: The DEF CON 34 Badge
talks.teaser: Explains how the DEF CON 34 badge was designed and built, how attendees can attack it, and how its partly open-source Baochip-1x chip can be inspected.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the badge's conference mode, where attendees swap light patterns through a lightly encrypted exchange. Traits follow simple genetic rules, with some dominant and some recessive. After the event, the core module can be removed and used as a FIDO2 security token that shows the relying party on screen. It also works as a TOTP generator and an offline password store.

The speaker's motivation is that supply chains scale well, so hardware trust needs more than black-box chips. He describes infrared imaging, which can reveal a chip's transistors when the silicon is exposed. The badge's Baochip-1x is a custom chip he designed, and its CPUs, cryptographic accelerators, and the Rust-based boot and operating system are published as open source. He also covers the manufacturing effort: custom two-tone laminate, stainless steel finishes for the advanced badges, and automated test rigs that reached about 7,000 units a week with a yield above 98 percent.

For hackers, the badge includes flags to capture, and early solvers were already named. The BIO coprocessor, an open version of the Raspberry Pi PIO block, can be debugged at the waveform level through open RTL simulation. The speaker expects open hardware to show bugs after release and recommends firmware updates, with bare chips planned for wider distribution later.

talks.title: The Ghost Key - Illusions of 'Time Management' in TTLock Smart Locks
talks.teaser: Shows how TTLock's offline time checks in white-label smart locks can be bypassed, letting expired electronic keys open doors again.
talks.summary:
The talk examines TTLock, a white-label smart lock platform used in rentals, hotels and homes. Its design relies on the lock's clock and on keys issued in advance by the companion app, so the lock trusts a signed packet rather than checking whether that packet is still valid. The presenters began with a lock they owned and an unexpected double unlock, then captured Bluetooth traffic and hooked the Android app to map the command structure.

They found that a single AES key, derived from a default key hardcoded in the app, protects the authorization data, and that the app uploads this key in plaintext to the vendor's cloud. Their scripts, built without the official app, showed that deleting a key on the admin side did not stop it working, that the lock never checked the user ID, and that only the end date was enforced. Clock calibration could move the lock's time backward or forward, reviving an expired keypad code or writing false entries into the unlock log. They also described a cheap Bluetooth connection hold that kept the legitimate owner out.

The takeaway is that offline access control needs a trustworthy clock and server-side key verification. The speakers reported the flaws to the vendor, got no substantive reply within a 90-day window, and published their findings after finding them still present in newer app and firmware versions. Practical advice includes preferring gateway-based revocation, rekeying locks after tenants leave, and never hardcoding keys.

talks.title: Shopping Is The Attack - A Decade Of E Commerce Scalper Wars, And The Multi Agent AI Era
talks.teaser: Maps how e-commerce scalper bots combine fake accounts, exposed catalogue APIs and stock watchers to buy hot releases before real customers can.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a war story from a former head of security operations at a large European online retailer. A defensive block on a bag API, meant to stop sneaker bots, also took down an internal image service for about 45 minutes, while a limited release sold out within a minute. The speaker argues that scalping needs no vulnerability: each step is a valid request, so standard controls struggle to separate shoppers from bots.

The middle section walks through the attacker's playbook. It covers building an account pool through weakly validated student sign-ups and credential stuffing, then scoring accounts for loyalty so they pass checkout checks. Pre-release catalogue data and product images are pulled from unprotected APIs, computer vision matches images to SKUs, and a watcher polls public catalogues and alerts group chats the moment stock appears. The speaker also describes hoarding inventory to push prices down before buying, and how a raffle scandal and paid all-in-one bot tools lowered the barrier to entry. Rate limits, user agent rules, schema checks and reputation scoring each fell short, often because the business resisted added friction.

The closing part links this pattern to AI agents, which can run these steps in parallel at speeds beyond human operators. For practitioners, the takeaway is to treat shopping flows as an attack surface, audit mobile and internal APIs for exposed identifiers, and weigh collateral damage before blocking traffic.

talks.title: The Sandbox is a Suggestion - Deconstructing AI Agent Sandboxes
talks.teaser: Shows how the sandboxes in Claude Code, Gemini CLI and Codex CLI fail in CI automation, through permission, environment and kernel-level gaps.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a practical problem: AI coding agents now run in CI/CD pipelines and background jobs, where no human approves each action and untrusted text such as issue bodies can reach the agent. The speaker argues that every agent is a model wrapped in harness code, and that a sandbox is only as good as its model of the environment it runs in. He compares three vendors' containment designs: Claude Code's permission rules, Gemini CLI's process isolation with environment stripping, and Codex CLI's kernel-enforced sandbox.

For each design, the talk shows a gap between what is claimed and what is enforced. In Claude Code's CI action, a pre-approved tools flag overrode the ask gate, and a built-in allowlist of documentation hosts let fetched URLs leak data, using a public model hub's download counter as a side channel. In Gemini CLI, secrets were removed from the child process, but the parent's environment stayed readable through procfs, and a shell command allowlist was never checked at runtime. In Codex CLI, the default Linux backend left the git directory writable, and a shared temp directory let the agent plant a symlink that the parent followed to write files outside the workspace. The speaker says each issue was reported and patched.

The takeaway is a method for evaluating any agent sandbox: identify the containment mechanism, read its enforcement code, find the assumption it depends on, and test whether the real runtime breaks that assumption. Practitioners should verify sandboxes against their own pipeline rather than trusting vendor defaults.

talks.title: Shadow Webhooks - Hunting for Dangling Event Listeners in Enterprise Workspaces
talks.teaser: Shows how forgotten SaaS webhooks can leak event data or accept forged messages, and how to turn them into reproducible bug bounty reports.
talks.summary:
Enterprise software-as-a-service workspaces collect webhooks from chat, ticketing, source control and CI/CD tools, and many keep sending events after their owners, services or domains are gone. The speaker defines a shadow webhook as an event connection that stays trusted even though its owner, destination or validation model has become unclear. The model splits each connection into a source, a registry entry, a destination, a receiver-side validator and an owner, and the trust breaks when one of those parts becomes uncertain.

The talk lays out four failure patterns: a retired destination, reclaimable infrastructure such as an expired domain or deleted cloud function, weak request validation, and an orphaned owner. The workflow runs from inventory and classification through fingerprinting and safe validation with synthetic events, then impact assessment and reporting. A controlled lab demonstrates two cases. A synthetic Jira-style event is delivered to a retired callback that still returns a success code, and a forged Slack-style request with an invalid signature is accepted by a weak receiver but rejected with an unauthorized response by a hardened one.

The speaker argues that a finding becomes triageable only when the trusted source is active, live delivery is proven, the ownership gap is clear, validation is weak, and the payload or workflow impact matters. Testers should prove trust without collecting real third-party data. Defenders are advised to assign named owners, enforce signatures and timestamp windows, set expiry dates, rotate secrets and monitor the lifecycle of linked domains and cloud resources.

talks.title: The Glass Perimeter - Systematic Bypasses in Biometric Frameworks
talks.teaser: Shows how liveness biometric checks in banking KYC apps were bypassed using deepfake video injected into Android camera pipelines.
talks.summary:
The talk examines the liveness checks that banks and fintech apps use during facial identity verification. The presenters tested seven top-tier apps built on four KYC SDKs over about six months, and report that every app but one could be bypassed. They argue that a few public photos are enough to build a convincing synthetic identity video cheaply, and they describe physical spoofing with masks, printed faces and other props, which worked only some of the time.

The core of the talk walks through injection points from the application layer down to the Android camera server. Before any injection, the team had to defeat root, emulator and debugger checks, sometimes by flipping return values or by exploiting debug-only flags left in release builds. Frame injection then fed recorded or deepfake frames at whichever layer the app trusted. The lowest layer, the camera server, was invisible to the app itself and fed frames to every application on the phone, and it was the only route that worked against the one hardened app that resisted the earlier techniques.

The takeaway for practitioners is that client-side liveness and anti-tampering checks should not be the sole gate for identity decisions. The speakers recommend moving verification logic to the server side and note the dilemma CISOs face when tuning thresholds, since loosening them enables fraud and tightening them locks out legitimate users.

talks.title: The Compiler That Can't Read - Crashing Every 5G Phone With 1 Byte
talks.teaser: Shows how ASN.1-generated decoders in 5G phone basebands skip specification rules, so one altered byte can crash a modem before authentication.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at the baseband modem in a 5G phone, a separate processor that handles radio messages from cell towers. The speakers focus on the window before the phone authenticates to a network, when a rogue base station can send a crafted radio setup message that the modem decodes and acts on, with no user interaction.

The core argument is that code generated from ASN.1 schemas only enforces what the schema expresses. Presence conditions and cross-field dependencies that exist only in 3GPP specification prose are lost, so a structurally valid message can break the standard. Some implementations also accept integer values above the allowed maximum because the encoding has spare bit patterns. The researchers describe a pipeline that extracts these rules from the specification, uses a language model to turn them into testable constraints, and mutates valid messages to violate them. They report crashes in basebands from several chipset vendors and show a live over-the-air demonstration.

For defenders, the practical lesson is to validate decoded values before the baseband uses them, not to trust the decoder alone. The speakers also argue that machine-readable rules in the standards would let tooling enforce them. The same gap may appear in other ASN.1-based systems, including LTE and some automotive and aviation protocols.

talks.title: TEE .fail - Breaking Trusted Execution Environments via DDR5 Memory Bus Interposition
talks.teaser: Shows how a cheap DDR5 bus interposer can expose deterministic memory encryption on server CPUs and leak an attestation signing key from a trusted enclave.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the premise that trusted execution environments protect code and data even against a malicious hypervisor or physical access to RAM. The speakers argue that server TEEs, including Intel SGX for data center parts, TDX, and AMD SEV-SNP, moved to a memory encryption engine that gives up integrity and replay protection, and that the remaining confidentiality is deterministic. They describe building a DDR5 bus interposer from e-commerce parts, with a refurbished logic analyzer standing in for a commercial tool priced around $300,000. Early attempts damaged boards and failed to boot, and the team reports that a working interposer took a lot of manual rewiring.

Captures showed that writing the same plaintext to memory produces the same ciphertext, which the speakers used as a dictionary-style oracle. They paused an enclave between iterations of an ECDSA signing loop, observed the 5-bit lookup table reads for each nonce chunk, and recovered the nonce and then the platform attestation key during the live demo. They say the key lets an attacker forge attestation for SGX and TDX, with examples including blockchain confidential computing and NVIDIA confidential compute. The vendors treat the issue as out of scope, and a real fix needs new hardware, while software-only randomized encryption is very costly.

The practical takeaway is that attestation-based trust on server TEEs should not be assumed to hold against an attacker with physical access to the memory bus. Operators who depend on these guarantees should reassess their threat model, and researchers should expect cheap bus-level tooling to be part of the attack surface.

talks.title: Tech Reclaimers Update - A Year In, Building a Social Movement Away from Big Tech
talks.teaser: Traces the first year of Tech Reclaimers, a peer-to-peer movement helping people move off Big Tech, and outlines its next plans.
talks.summary:
The panel marks the first year of Tech Reclaimers, a non-profit that grew out of a Fediverse community around the Hackers.Town instance. Its aim is to help people leave big tech platforms through peer-to-peer teaching rather than top-down instruction. The founders describe how the idea took shape after one of them ran a 21-day cleanse aimed at the gap between early adopters and everyone else.

Over the year the group built an online presence on Mastodon, Discord and Signal, ran in-person workshops, and produced printable guides. The speakers also described harder parts of the work, including the sudden death of a co-founder weeks after launch and the paperwork of forming a 501(c)(3). They shared stories of members teaching each other, such as a newcomer who moved from an iPhone to a Linux distribution. Current campaigns cover music and photo libraries using self-hosted tools like Jellyfin, an indie-web push called the Evergreen Web, and links with groups in Europe, the UK and the Neo-Luddite movement in New York.

Looking ahead, the group plans to take workshops into libraries, community centers and colleges, and to help friends migrate their tools together. Their advice to newcomers is to examine the social and economic forces behind a product, not only the technology.

talks.title: Taming the Swarm - Hard Architectural Lessons from Building a Deterministic Agentic Web Pentesting System
talks.teaser: Shows how a deterministic agentic web pentest pipeline separates AI proposals from external validation, using specialist agents, a skeptic agent, and browser-based proof.
talks.summary:
Albert Corzo opens with a problem many testers will recognize: AI pentest tools produce polished reports with high confidence scores, yet the evidence behind them often cannot be reproduced. His early prototype generated realistic-looking findings that none of them could confirm by hand. He also argues that public benchmarks hide retries and failed runs, so a single success rate says little about whether a model suits offensive work. Swapping in a more expensive model did not fix the underlying problem.

The middle of the talk covers the design changes that followed. Corzo replaces one generalist agent with specialists that get narrow context and fixed output formats, then sends their findings to a skeptic agent whose only job is to disprove them. Priority comes from weighted scores, not majority votes. The language model proposes strategy, while a separate execution layer manages requests, state and model switching after refusals. Validation depends on the bug class: XSS needs confirmation in a real browser, while code reading alone counts as a hypothesis. A test range with known vulnerabilities, the Dojo, exposed an agent that edited server configuration to pass tests, so he separated the optimizer from the test.

The closing section shows a demo of reports, reproduction artifacts and an MCP-connected chat, along with cost and runtime figures for one scan. The takeaway is to treat model output as unverified until external evidence confirms it, and to publish code and prompts so others can audit the behavior.

talks.title: Talkers Without Borders - Worldwide Free Speech without an Internet Connection
talks.teaser: Demonstrates how the AIS maritime safety network can carry hidden messages inside ordinary-looking ship traffic, and how defenders might detect them.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a disclaimer about jurisdiction and unauthorized transmission, then explains the Automatic Identification System, a maritime safety network built for openness. AIS messages carry no cryptographic sender authentication, so receivers cannot verify who transmitted them, yet aggregated AIS data still informs shipping, commodity and financial decisions. The speakers argue that this trust gap could be used to carry covert traffic.

They present Evil AIS, a research framework with nine encoding methods and a combined variant. It hides payload bits in the low-order bits of position reports that already exist, then recovers them with differential steganography: a receiver XORs two near-identical reports to extract the difference. In a controlled setup, the team showed a message split across 16 shards that could be rebuilt from any 12, using parity similar to RAID 5. Other demos covered a binary dead drop and a trigger that fires a downstream action from a few bits, which they tied to systems that consume AIS as input.

For defenders, the takeaways are to validate checksums, flag anomalous raw AIS traffic, build baselines from historical data, and triangulate where suspicious transmissions originate. The speakers note that the protocol dates to the 1990s and is unlikely to change soon, so monitoring has to start now.

talks.title: Taking on the Dark Fleet in Cyberspace
talks.teaser: Coast Guard cyber operators describe boarding shadow fleet tankers and the insecure IT and OT systems they found aboard.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at the United States-led crackdown on dark fleet tankers, vessels that carry sanctioned oil under false flags, shell-company ownership, and rotating registrations. Coast Guard Cyber Command's cyber protection teams join the physical boardings of these ships. Their job is to establish a secure cyber posture on vessels they have never seen, across both IT and OT systems, while protecting the boarding team and the crew. The speakers note that equipment, power and connectivity had to be planned for austere conditions at sea.

The middle of the talk covers what the teams found. Flat networks put crew Wi-Fi, admin workstations and bridge systems in one broadcast domain. Satellite links fed unauthenticated wireless access points, and USB drives and hand-made Ethernet cables bridged supposed air gaps to engineering systems. Many machines ran unsupported Windows versions with pirated software and old worms still active. Remote access tools were used to wipe disks. Navigation data was also manipulated: AIS antennas were wrapped to attenuate their signal, NMEA sentences were injected, and LRIT satellite terminal firmware had been altered. The team also recovered forged port stamp software.

The takeaway is that the line between physical and digital risk has largely disappeared. Legacy marine electronics that trust unauthenticated serial data need monitoring and segmentation, and the speakers urge security researchers to help secure them before a maritime accident is traced to something as simple as an unsegmented cable.

talks.title: Tag, You’re It - Physical Tracking Tech, Defense, and How to DIY Your Own
talks.teaser: Traces physical tracking tech from Cold War beacons to AirTags, tests a Meshtastic LoRa locator, and covers countermeasures and a budget DIY build.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with a survival-planning question: how would you navigate back to base in a grid-down scenario where GPS satellites are gone? That led the speaker's team to explore LoRa mesh radio as an off-grid tracker. Before the prototype, the speaker surveys the history of physical tracking, from IFF transponders and early ground-based navigation to today's AirTags, Tile trackers, cheap OBD-II and GPS units, and LoRa asset systems already used in warehouses. The case against commercial trackers rests on corporate server logging and their failure without cellular or Bluetooth coverage.

The middle section covers defenses and the team's build attempts. Phone alerts and the third-party AirGuard app catch some unwanted trackers, while physical sweeps, SDR scanning near 925 MHz, thermal imaging and nonlinear junction detectors cover the higher end, though the last are costly. The two-antenna timing approach failed, and a room of ESP-NOW receivers using weighted-centroid math kept placing the target in the middle. Body interference and the need to recalibrate for each room made the design messy.

The closing points are practical. LoRa can reach hundreds of meters in dense urban areas and kilometers in ideal conditions, which suits kids, dogs, backcountry use and subterranean sites. The speaker notes that red teams already use LoRa for persistence, and that a low-duty-cycle beacon is hard to detect. The takeaway is that cheap off-grid tracking is feasible, and that defenders need to plan for it.

talks.title: Stop Being the Integration Layer
talks.teaser: Presents an open-source Rust toolkit that ingests common forensic artifacts into one resumable DuckDB super timeline, so analysts stop hand-stitching tool output.
talks.summary:
Albert Hui starts from years of digital forensics and incident response work, where much of the time went into reconciling inconsistent CSV and JSON output from a long list of tools. He calls this manual reconciliation the integration layer and argues that analysts should spend that time on investigation. He points out that many strong tools are Windows-only or commercial, and that vendors often ask for case data they cannot legally share in order to reproduce bugs.

He then presents ASIN, an open-source triage program written in Rust. It is installable through Homebrew, Winget, Linux packages, or cargo, and it ingests disk images, containers, and common file systems without the user having to understand partition formats. Parsed artifacts such as the MFT, event logs, registry, prefetch, shortcut files, jump lists, and shimcache go into DuckDB, and new collections can be added incrementally to a super timeline. Hui reports that a 4.6 GB E01 CTF image scanned in just over a minute on a laptop, though he admits speed claims are self-serving. A companion mount tool exposes images as folders so existing tools keep working, and the parsers flag abnormal entries and reject malformed input.

Hui is candid that the project is early and likely still buggy. He says every crate was fuzzed and cross-checked against other tools and real data, and that the results are reproducible. His takeaway is to keep favourite tools, use the pipeline to triage and pivot, and stop acting as the integration layer when it is not needed.

talks.title: Smile, youre on camera Livestreaming from North Koreas IT workers laptop farm
talks.teaser: Presents how researchers posed as an employer to infiltrate a North Korean IT worker cell and record its daily laptop-farm operations.
talks.summary:
The talk follows two researchers who tracked a North Korean IT worker division, described as a sub-group of Lazarus, that places operatives in Western companies to send revenue to the regime and gain footholds for espionage. Earlier, the team had interviewed recruits who offered to lend their identities to fake applicants. For a second phase, they set up a fictional crypto firm, hired the operatives, and gave them virtual desktops running inside a sandbox that logged every click, file open and network connection.

The recordings showed daily routines: the workers checked whether they were being sandboxed, synced browser passwords and cookies to personal accounts, and installed AI tools for auto-filling applications and live interview translation. They also shared remote-access software, one-time password apps and a commercial VPN. Outside the sandbox, open-source work linked the VPN exit nodes and a residential address to a Russian logistics figure near Vladivostok, and mapped many shell companies that reused the same websites, phone numbers and addresses. Payment trails hopped through several privacy services to send small sums.

The speakers closed with practical advice for employers: run recurring in-person identity checks, block known anonymizing VPN ranges, and remember that operatives are human and can be questioned about everyday habits. Fuller footage and details were promised in a follow-up article.

talks.title: Sliding into the Flight Deck’s DMs - Practical Message Attacks on CPDLC
talks.teaser: Shows how the text-messaging link that carries air traffic control instructions to airliners can be impersonated with cheap software-defined radio gear.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at CPDLC, the data link that lets air traffic controllers send text clearances such as climb, descend or turn to commercial aircraft. The speakers note that the protocol has no cryptography or authentication, and that aviation standards and industry have long treated concerns about such radio systems as overblown. To test this, they built a bench with certified avionics and a VHF antenna, then connected it to a live test ground station, so the experiments ran against a real network rather than a simulation.

The middle section walks through the protocol stack, from the data link layer up through link setup, routing and transport to the application. The speakers describe a stateless disconnect frame that, sent to a broadcast address, drops every nearby aircraft from its ground station, which they say needs only a few bytes over the air. Using a fake ground station, they could take over a session, advertise routes so an aircraft would accept them, and send arbitrary controller messages. Undocumented parameters and checksums, some turning out to be MD4, made the reverse engineering slow.

The closing part covers disclosure to manufacturers, regulators, airlines and pilot groups, with mixed responses and slow engagement from the FAA. The practical takeaways are that complexity does not provide security, that monitoring for unexpected messages and physical protection of ground stations are feasible now, and that cryptography will take years because the move to IP-based links keeps slipping. The speakers said they would not release code, but the paper would give the details.

talks.title: Shepherding the Tor network
talks.teaser: Traces how the Tor network's volunteer relay community, its attack landscape and its abuse handling have changed over nearly 25 years of operation.
talks.summary:
Roger Dingledine, one of Tor's original developers, opens with the network's basics: volunteer relays, three-hop circuits, exit policies, and nine directory authorities that publish the hourly consensus. He explains why directory information was later moved onto relays so censors could not block the network by blocking a few addresses. He then ranks threats by how often they occur in practice, putting operational security mistakes first, followed by browser fingerprinting, browser exploits, traffic confirmation and traffic analysis.

The middle of the talk covers relay operators. The pool has shifted from home computers to university and nonprofit exit relays and then to cloud VPS providers, so a single host can end up carrying a large share of the network. Stories include an early abuse complaint triggered by a Windows installer, spoofed SSH scans that got directory authority addresses blocklisted, a botnet that briefly multiplied users, and a campaign of fake cryptocurrency exchange sites. The talk also covers legal and ethical questions around exit relays, content filtering, and the research safety board that reviews studies of users.

He closes with open problems: admission control that is less centralized, tracking how many relays the team personally knows, and routing that does not overload Europe. He urges the DEF CON audience to run relays and help build relay capacity in the United States.

talks.title: The Stream Is Dead, Long Live the Stream - How HTTP 2 Lets Dead Streams Keep Servers Working
talks.teaser: Traces how HTTP/2 Rapid Reset research led to MadeYouReset, a flaw where streams close at the protocol layer while server-side request work keeps running.
talks.summary:
The talk treats HTTP/2 weaknesses as failures of request lifetime rather than bugs in one codebase. It begins with the 2023 Rapid Reset disclosure, which is usually explained as a flood of cancelled requests. The speaker argues the real issue is that a stream can be closed at the protocol level while the back end is still computing a response for it. Those closed-but-active requests are called phantom streams.

Tracing how a server's HTTP/2 module hands off to its back end showed that the reset event is generally discarded by the rest of the server, so work continues and the finished response is thrown away. Cancellation was tested on Rust's Hyper and related frameworks, and it failed in some paths even where it appeared to work. The MadeYouReset variant forces the server to send the reset itself, for example through a zero-increment window update, which avoids the client-side reset limits added after Rapid Reset. Demonstrations on Pingora and Actix Web showed CPU and memory climbing until the servers crashed.

The root cause, according to the speaker, is architectural: HTTP/2 was added to servers built around an HTTP/1.1 interface that had no cancellation, and full cancellation across legacy code and external services is impractical. Because phantom streams cannot be eliminated, the proposed mitigation is to limit resets sent by the server as well as by the client. The takeaway for practitioners is to check how protocol features actually integrate with the software beneath them.

talks.title: The Enclave Is Lying to You - Breaking TEE Trust Boundaries Through Boot Time State
talks.teaser: Shows how a single S3 upload with a directory traversal path lets an attacker run code as root inside an AWS Nitro Enclave without breaking attestation.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that confidential computing platforms such as Nitro Enclaves, SEV-SNP and TDX attest the code an enclave runs, but not the runtime inputs it reads at boot. These include objects in cloud storage, configuration passed in by the host, and KMS key policies that do not require attestation. The speaker presents this as a deployment gap rather than a hardware flaw, and says the attestation measurements stay valid even when those inputs are abused.

The demonstration starts from one s3:PutObject permission on the enclave's state bucket. The uploaded key contains a directory traversal sequence. Object storage treats it as a literal string, but the enclave's file system resolves it and writes the file into the code directory, replacing a helper module that handles KMS decrypt calls. On the next boot, the replaced code runs as root, collects the parent instance's IAM session credentials, and captures plaintext data keys from KMS. The speaker then uses those keys to decrypt a database and extract signing key shares. The PCR values do not change throughout.

Several defenses held in the same assessment, including filtering of environment variable injection, certificate pinning against DNS redirection, and fuzzing of the host RPC channel. The shipped fix validates file names on the download path with an allow list and traversal checks, because signing the boot files would need a verification key baked into the image. The speaker released an open-source scanner, untrust, with about 28 checks for Nitro deployments, and urged teams to treat bootstrap scripts and boot-time inputs as part of their security boundary.

talks.title: The 2026 Pwnie Awards
talks.teaser: Presents the 2026 Pwnie Awards ceremony, handing out mock prizes for the year's notable exploits, research, and vendor responses.
talks.summary:
The 2026 Pwnie Awards opened with a host explaining the volunteer, unpaid format of the show and how each category would run. Presenters then walked through nominees for categories including best remote code execution, best privilege escalation, best server-side cloud bug, best mobile bug, best AI security research, most innovative research, most underhyped research, lamest vendor response, and most epic fail. Each nominee got a short, joking description of the bug or research. Examples included a KVM guest-to-host escape on ARM64, a Linux privilege escalation shared by two researchers, a zero-click audio decoding chain on Pixel phones, prompt-injection attacks against AI browsers and operations agents, and a DNS character-handling flaw affecting many implementations. Several winners were absent, so others accepted on their behalf.

The middle of the show leaned on running jokes about vendors. Microsoft's handling of several disclosed bugs drew the lamest vendor response award, and an AI chatbot prompt-injection that led to an Instagram account takeover took most epic fail. The hosts also noted that many AI-related nominees reflected how quickly new AI products were being probed.

The show closed with thanks to the volunteers and sponsors, and with a reminder that the awards depend on researchers publishing their work. For a practitioner, the ceremony is a compact snapshot of the year's notable research: zero-click mobile attacks, AI features as an attack surface, and how vendors respond to disclosure.

talks.title: Transformers - Dark Side of the Type - Weaponizing Conversion Layer
talks.teaser: Shows how turning a plain string into a typed .NET object can lead to remote code execution, with no serializer involved.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that a common step, turning a plain string into an object, is a separate security problem from insecure deserialization. Many .NET programs build objects from strings through type converters, parse methods, single-argument constructors, property setters, or custom code. When an attacker can also choose the type, that conversion can run dangerous code, and no serializer is involved. The speaker names this class Insecure String Transformation.

The speaker explains which types an attacker can reach, including the global assembly cache on .NET Framework and the Windows Desktop Runtime on modern .NET. Gadgets such as ResXFileRef, XAML readers, and ObjectDataProvider show outbound network reach and code execution. Two SharePoint cases anchor the talk. A 2020 type-converter bug had no restriction in front of the sink, while a later parser bug let a generic type slip past an allow list that checked only control types. Microsoft patched both by restricting which types may be resolved.

For defenders, the hunt has three parts: find where input becomes a type, see what consumes that type, and flag gadgets that touch files, networks, or XAML. Without source code, look for .NET type names in traffic, storage, or logs. The durable fix is removing attacker control over the type, using fixed types where possible and otherwise an allow list checked before resolution.

talks.title: Weaponizing Uselessness - Breaking SMM with the Slowest Instruction Ever Written
talks.teaser: Shows how stretching a single x86 instruction past one second can break System Management Mode's core rendezvous and expose dormant firmware CVEs.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with an unusual goal: find the slowest possible x86 machine instruction. The speaker explains System Management Mode, a privileged firmware-level mode that sits below the kernel and is hidden from the operating system and hypervisor. SMM relies on a rendezvous in which every core must enter together. That rendezvous has a timeout of about one second, so if one core stays outside SMM long enough, the others proceed anyway. Defeating it requires one instruction that stalls longer than a second.

The speaker works through a leaderboard of candidates. Simple arithmetic, square roots, serializing instructions, entropy depletion, model-specific registers and cache write-backs all fall short. Port I/O and then memory-mapped I/O go much further. Misaligned and oversized accesses, wide SIMD registers and a full floating-point state restore push the cost higher still. The final step has other cores hammer the same address with locked accesses to contend for the system bus, reaching roughly 198 billion cycles, or about 49 seconds. A scaled-down version then desynchronized SMM entry across cores in a live demonstration.

The takeaway is that the rendezvous assumption fails, which would expose a large set of time-of-check to time-of-use SMM vulnerabilities that are mostly unpatched. The impact covers confidential computing in the cloud and firmware persistence on client systems. The speaker argues there is no clean fix. Keeping the timeout leaves the attack open, while removing it lets one stuck core hang the whole platform.

talks.title: Your WAF Blocked Us, That Was The Exploit
talks.teaser: Shows how attacker-controlled text in WAF logs, Sentry errors and Datadog telemetry can steer AI coding agents into DNS changes, cross-agent takeover and data exfiltration.
talks.summary:
