The speakers argue that AI agents cannot separate data from instructions, so any untrusted text that reaches an agent's context, such as logs or error reports, can act as a command. They start with Sentry. Public DSNs embedded in front-end JavaScript let anyone submit an error event, and the message field accepts markdown that the Sentry MCP passes to the agent unchanged. A crafted error can therefore persuade a Claude Code session to run an attacker-chosen package. They extend the idea to Seer, Sentry's hosted agent. Injected breadcrumbs make Seer recommend installing a package, and Cursor trusts that recommendation more than raw input, so one agent compromises another.

The Cloudflare chain begins with a request that a managed WAF rule blocks. The payload sits in the user-agent header, which the MCP returns, while the body that triggered the block stays hidden. An agent reviewing blocked requests then treats the user-agent text as troubleshooting facts and used Cloudflare's own MCP tools to add a DNS record. No code ran on the victim machine. The speakers also describe a Claude sandbox escape: the egress proxy accepted a JWT that was not bound to a container, so an attacker-minted token allowed traffic to arbitrary domains. Anthropic has since fixed it. For persistence, they describe poisoning memory files, skills and MCP configuration, which existing EDR and WAF tooling would not flag.

Their takeaways are to limit which MCPs and external domains agents can reach, to treat all externally sourced data as contaminated, to enforce egress controls at runtime, to require human approval for high-risk actions, and to audit agent memory and config files for tampering.

talks.title: Very Pwned - Hacking Verifone’s Card Machine Three Times in a Row
talks.teaser: Shows how a Verifone P400+ payment terminal fell to three successive root exploit chains, and how root access exposed card data.
talks.summary:
The talk follows an assessor who tested Verifone P400+ payment terminals during yearly PCI assessments. Each year the speaker found a new route to root after the vendor patched the previous one. The first foothold was a command injection in the file manager, triggered by a crafted MP3 filename, which gave a low-privilege shell. A later firmware update path let an archive be extracted in a way that wrote files outside the staging directory before signature checks ran.

The research continued through an unauthenticated recovery environment, a point-of-sale protocol that allowed file reads and writes, and HTML rendering that passed filenames unsafely to a media player. Further chains abused a privileged broker, a downgrade of a patched component, and a web server started from a writable location. With root, the speaker disabled the kernel's role-based access control, kept a persistent backdoor by recalculating the integrity hash of the protected filesystem, and ran Doom in a chroot.

The final section showed that plaintext card track data and account numbers appeared in process traces and memory dumps, despite the device's secure-world design. The vendor fixed most issues, but the card data exposure remained for this end-of-sale model. The practical takeaways are to patch terminals regularly, not to rely on certification alone, and to push vendors for more openness about device security.

talks.title: Thin Client - Thin Crypto Bypassing Full-Disk Encryption Across 3 Thin Clients - wo Breaking a Cipher
talks.teaser: Shows how full disk encryption on Dell, HP and IGEL thin clients falls to boot chain and TPM flaws, letting an attacker reach the disk from a powered-off device.
talks.summary:
Thin clients run full operating systems and hold Wi-Fi keys, 802.1X certificates, admin password hashes and VDI configuration, yet their disk encryption is often tied to the TPM. The speaker examined three vendors: IGEL OS (formerly Eagle), HP ThinPro and Dell ThinOS, across several major versions. Because the TPM releases its key only after the bootloader and kernel load, those early boot stages were the main target.

IGEL had a sound design that seals keys to PCR values, but a boot menu entry and an unsigned configuration partition let the speaker reach a root shell. A missing signature file also dropped the device to a GRUB prompt. HP ThinPro measured only part of the boot chain, so the unseal script could be modified to write out the key. Dell's older ThinOS releases had weaker schemes: an administrator password was obfuscated with a reused XOR key that could be recovered from SPI flash, and a key derived from hardware identifiers was used in place of measurement. ThinOS 9 also wrote crash dumps unencrypted. ThinOS 10 released its key from TPM storage with no policy at all, and a later PCR 7 fix could be sidestepped with another Canonical-signed USB stick.

The main lesson is that automatically unsealed disk encryption is hard to get right, and TPM-only protection fails when the boot partition is not measured. The speaker urged assessors to read the boot scripts rather than assume encryption is effective. At the time of the talk, the HP issue was reported as unpatched.

talks.title: You've Got Mail That Was Meant For No One
talks.teaser: Shows how unowned placeholder email domains quietly collect misdirected sensitive mail from companies and government agencies.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with a domain registered on a whim that had a catch-all mailbox. Over time the speaker began receiving misdirected mail: a city government's faxed forms with personal data, pizza orders, billing messages, ticketing alerts, and developer test credentials. The senders had used addresses like "no reply" as placeholders, and the mail kept arriving once the domains were free to register.

The speaker then registered other domains, including a .net variant that drew far more traffic, and tracked volumes, senders, and attachments over several years. To map the problem, he wrote a Python tool that checks mail servers for catch-all acceptance using only SMTP handshakes, without sending content, and stores results in SQLite. Across 328 prefixes covering about 7,000 domains, roughly 8.4 percent were confirmed as catch-alls. He named this practice placeholder squatting and compared it with earlier public reports of similar addresses.

The takeaway is that placeholder values in test accounts, IoT devices, or deletion workflows become liabilities if their domains lapse. Developers should use reserved domains or the .invalid TLD, and sysadmins should audit their mail systems and logs for misdirected traffic.

talks.title: Your Bank Thinks I'm You - A Kill Chain Against Mobile Banking Security
talks.teaser: Shows how a chain of bypasses defeated root detection, Frida hooks, KYC liveness checks, and anti-deepfake controls in mobile banking apps.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through a full attack chain against mobile banking and digital wallet apps used in a Latin American market, with the testing described as done in an authorized setting. The presenter frames the defenses as four stacked layers: runtime self-protection with root and integrity checks, anti-instrumentation, biometric identity verification with liveness detection, and anti-deepfake controls. The attack moves through them in order, starting with hiding a rooted device using freely available kernel-level modules and integrity-spoofing tools.

The middle section covers the Frida-based stage. By hooking the biometric SDK's image retrieval call, the researchers swapped the captured frame for a chosen image before the SDK packaged and signed it. Where the SDK added metadata and encoding, they rebuilt the same template on the client so the backend received a consistent payload. The liveness check ran entirely on the phone, so a real face could pass it while a different photo was submitted for matching. They also generated synthetic faces from ID photos with consumer AI tools, reporting that none were flagged by the anti-deepfake controls across their trials.

The closing part argues that the weakness is architectural: each layer trusts the one before it, and client-side checks cannot carry the decision. Suggested fixes include server-side validation of liveness, cryptographic binding of captured media, and behavioral analysis. The presenter also notes that criminal KYC bypass toolkits are sold online and that the demo videos could not be shown on stage.

talks.title: Attacking the Trust Boundary Where SMS Meets the Internet
talks.teaser: Shows how an SMS gateway's trust assumptions and code bugs let attackers suppress, forge, and read one-time passcodes in transit.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a practical question: what happens when a one-time passcode sent through a bank's SMS path never reaches the phone. The speakers focus on Kannel, an open-source SMS and WAP gateway first released in 1999, whose last stable release they date to 2018 and which still carries bank traffic. They describe its process layout, where the central engine accepts connections from other components on an unauthenticated TCP port, and why its outbound TLS does not validate certificates.

Using a lab with a fake bank application, a log observer, and a rogue carrier built with Osmo software, they demonstrate silent message suppression, forged delivery receipts that enable billing fraud, and a message-ID conversion mismatch that can misroute receipts. They also show a null-byte discrepancy that hides content from logs, direct SMS injection through the open port, command injection through a keyword-triggered exec feature, and a SQL injection that reaches command execution. Legacy protocol parsers contain classic memory corruption as well.

The takeaway is that these weaknesses stem from design trust assumptions as much as aging code, so patching individual bugs will not fully fix them. Operators should keep gateway ports off the internet, restrict access, and monitor backend logs rather than relying only on front-end records.

talks.title: Zero Day Provisioning - Chaining TP Link ZTP Vulns
talks.teaser: Dissects TP-Link Omada zero-touch provisioning protocols and shows how 17 flaws let attackers impersonate controllers and clients to infiltrate networks.
talks.summary:
Zero-touch provisioning (ZTP) lets administrators onboard and configure network devices remotely, without a technician on site. The speakers from Forescout argue that this convenience rests on implicit trust, with a central controller as a single point of failure and proprietary protocols that vendors design without a standard. They picked TP-Link's Omada ecosystem because little public research covered it. To study it, they rooted client gateways through the web interface and reverse engineered the controller software, then mapped the discovery and adoption phases.

The protocol analysis turned up a chain of weaknesses. A legacy protocol version could be forced on controllers. Session keys had too little entropy to resist passive decryption, and the authentication hash could be captured and cracked offline. Keys and certificates were hard-coded, so one extracted certificate let a fake controller pass the chain-of-trust check. Factory default credentials during provisioning let an impersonated client be adopted, and the controller then handed out site credentials. Cloud adoption depended only on predictable serial numbers and was not bound to a state machine, which enabled a race condition, a stored XSS, and a content security policy bypass for phishing. Live demos showed a local root takeover and a remote phishing attack.

The vendor took 426 days to fix the issues, and 13 of the 17 received CVEs. The speakers recommend that vendors follow standards and avoid hard-coded keys, and that users enable multi-factor authentication, change defaults, rotate credentials and VPN keys, and apply updates.

talks.title: Hybrid Quantum ML for Passive OS Fingerprinting
talks.teaser: Shows how passive OS fingerprinting can run on a 20-qubit quantum classifier and be benchmarked against XGBoost on CIC-IDS 2017 packet captures.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at passive operating system fingerprinting, which identifies the OS behind captured network traffic without sending any probes to the target. The speaker uses nPrint to convert packet captures into binary feature columns, then removes identifying fields such as IP addresses so a model cannot simply memorize the answers. The classical baseline is the XGBoost gradient-boosting model from the open-source OSIRIS-ML tool.

The core experiment swaps that classifier for a hybrid quantum-classical model. Each of 20 binary features is encoded into one of 20 qubits, the qubits are linked in a linear entanglement layout, and the measured outputs feed a small classical neural network that predicts among 12 OS classes. Over 50 training epochs on a simulator, the quantum model reached a weighted F1 of 0.348 against 0.361 for XGBoost on the same features, with accuracy of 42.9% versus 45.85%. It used about 1,228 trainable parameters, compared with more than 33,000 for the baseline.

The speaker is clear about the limits: the runs used a simulator rather than noisy hardware, some training runs collapsed, and the circuit was small. A classical baseline built on the top 20 features from a much larger set scored about 49%. The takeaway is that quantum machine learning can be applied to security workloads beyond cryptography, and that the method can be reproduced on a modern GPU. Larger circuits, continuous features and real quantum hardware are named as next steps.

talks.title: Writing to Shadow Stacks
talks.teaser: Shows three ways to write attacker-chosen return addresses into Linux shadow stacks, undermining Intel CET and ARM GCS backward-edge protection.
talks.summary:
Shadow stacks, as in Intel CET and ARM GCS, are meant to make return-address corruption a dead end by keeping a hardware-checked second copy of return addresses. The talk asks whether that copy can be written from user space. It starts with how the kernel marks and installs shadow stack pages, and why certain kernel write paths can reach them.

The speaker then presents three bypasses. The first abuses the /proc/self/mem write path, where a force flag lets a process write to its own shadow stack pages with open() and pwrite(). The second uses userfaultfd: a shadow stack page is discarded with MADV_DONTNEED, and a fault handler supplies a replacement page filled with chosen return addresses, because the copy path skips a check that the move path enforces. The third uses the WRSSQ instruction, and the speaker corrects a widely copied encoding that actually decodes to a different instruction. The techniques were validated on Sapphire Rapids and against CVEs in dnsmasq, libinput and rsync, including a root shell with CET still enabled.

The first two kernel paths were patched after disclosure, though a fork-and-ptrace variant still works on patched kernels and WRSSQ is a CPU instruction that cannot be patched. The speaker argues that memory management gaps in subsystems written before kernel 6.6 remain a concern, and suggests sealing shadow stack mappings as a mitigation. Practitioners should treat the backward edge as writable on some systems and keep older exploitation techniques in mind.

talks.title: Wrestling with a Python - Escaping Copilot Studio's AI Guarded Sandbox
talks.teaser: Shows how an attacker escapes the Python sandbox behind Microsoft Copilot Studio's code interpreter, then defeats the LLM guardrail that screens the code.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with Microsoft Copilot Studio, where agents can run Python through a code interpreter. The presenters treat that interpreter as a target. Behind it sit a Windows container on Azure Service Fabric, a Python sandbox, and a small language model that decides whether each piece of code is safe to run. They picked the smallest model in the settings, expecting it to be the easiest to get past.

Early probes used module introspection and file-reading helpers to reach sandbox internals and TLS material. The guardrail turned out to be non-deterministic: the same payload sometimes passed and sometimes failed. Its API responses also echoed its security reasoning, which gave the team feedback for refining payloads. Walking Python's method resolution order got around the dunder filters. The team then found a hard-coded administrator credential in a related Dataverse plugin environment that also appeared in the Copilot containers, and it cracked quickly. The haul included certificates, private keys, around 75 environment variables, and application source, along with command execution as a container user.

Microsoft first rated the reports low severity. The speakers said the escape still worked in some environments after the tickets were marked fixed, and they released their tooling. The takeaways: sandboxing untrusted code is hard, LLM-based guardrails are fallible, and organizations should keep sensitive data out of agent sandboxes.

talks.title: Witchcraft Solver - Automated 0day Discovery in Stripped Binaries
talks.teaser: Shows an automated pipeline that lifts stripped binaries to LLVM bytecode, runs static and symbolic analyzers over them, and uses fuzzing and concolic execution to turn candidate bugs into proofs of concept.
talks.summary:
The talk presents Witchcraft Solver, a pipeline that takes a stripped ELF binary with no source, symbols or harness and searches it for bugs. The speaker opens with a long digression on the limits of formal reasoning and AI claims, then argues that the practical problem is getting from a binary to a candidate vulnerability and then to a working exploit input.

The pipeline lifts binaries to LLVM bytecode using several open-source lifters. Function boundaries are recovered from exception-handling frame sections instead of relying on IDA. Sink functions come from sanitizer backtraces produced by OSS-Fuzz and ARVO. The bytecode then goes to several symbolic and abstract-interpretation analyzers, and an LLM triages the reports. On FFmpeg, about 26 candidates were flagged, and the triage separated false positives from a few real memory corruptions. A comparison on a libjpeg-turbo bug with no public exploit contrasts coverage-based fuzzing, directed fuzzing and concolic execution on a stripped binary.

The closing section looks at future work toward machine-checked proofs and at the preservation of vulnerability records, including the revival of the BugTraq mailing list. A demonstration of a type-confusion flaw in the Lean prover makes the point that proof tools also have bugs. The takeaway is that binary-only pipelines can reach real programs, but their output still needs human or formal verification.

talks.title: Welcome to DEF CON 34
talks.teaser: Opens DEF CON 34 with the founder's welcome, covering how the event is organized, its community norms, this year's agency theme, and milestone anniversaries.
talks.summary:
The founder opens DEF CON 34 by asking first-timers and returning attendees to raise their hands, then explains how the conference works as a set of smaller communities. With roughly 27,000 people present, he describes how villages and hands-on activities such as lock picking or robot hacking split attendees into small groups where they can meet people who share their interests. He says there is no single correct way to attend and encourages people to make a few plans a day and expect many side trips.

He traces the event's inclusive culture to its early years, when people judged each other by their ideas because there were no photos or video. He explains how the code of conduct was written down, how a safety team was formed, and why a public transparency report was published to earn trust. A disinvitation dispute that went to court is cited as an example of following through on those commitments. This year's theme is agency, which he frames as self-determination and community support during fast, AI-driven change.

He closes with anniversaries: 20 years of the electronic badge, 30 years of capture the flag, and the first year under new CTF organizers. He also notes that an AI agent won a challenge last year without its operator realizing it, which raises open questions about the future of CTF. The takeaway he gives is to try unfamiliar things, admit mistakes, and look for your community rather than chasing career credentials.

talks.title: WASM Was Not the Boundary - Sandcastles, Not Sandboxes
talks.teaser: Shows how untrusted Python running in a Pyodide WebAssembly sandbox escapes into Node.js or Deno host runtimes through ctypes and reflection.
talks.summary:
This talk examines Pyodide, a CPython interpreter compiled to WebAssembly with Emscripten, which several products use as a sandbox for running untrusted Python. The presenters tested seven products spanning workflow automation, spreadsheets, AI agent frameworks, CI build tooling, and desktop wrappers. In most of them, denylists blocked modules such as os and subprocess, but ctypes stayed importable, and class-hierarchy traversal could recover an import function even when it was not.

With ctypes, the escaped code can load the Emscripten exports of the process, pull out functions that run scripts, declare their signatures, and execute JavaScript on the host. On Node.js this gives immediate code execution. On Deno the outcome depends on the granted permissions, and one default configuration still reached full remote code execution. In CI, the escaped code runs beside tokens, signing keys, and release artifacts. The team reported seven escapes and four CVEs, and vendor responses varied, from archiving projects to calling the issue the deployer's responsibility.

The main takeaway is that denylists fail at the architectural level. The presenters recommended blocking ctypes at import, compiling out script-running exports, blocking reflection gadgets, and exporting only the functions an application needs. They also advised layering permissions and containers, and checking whether ctypes is importable, which host runtime is used, and which permissions are granted.

talks.title: Tracking the Trackers - How We Took Over 36M GPS Devices
talks.teaser: Shows how three GPS tracking platforms behind child watches and vehicle trackers let account holders reach devices, owners' data, and backend servers.
talks.summary:
The talk covers consumer GPS trackers sold as child watches and vehicle trackers. The researchers examine three platforms, SETracker, SinoTrack, and TKSTAR/Thinkrace, which they say reach tens of millions of devices across dozens of white-label brands that share the same Chinese backends. They start from a cheap tracker bought online and a companion app, then show that request signing was weak and that the server never checked which command was being sent, so any account holder could issue almost any device command.

Across the platforms they describe harvesting device IDs and parent emails from sequential user IDs with no rate limiting, then using commands for silent audio monitoring, camera capture, overwriting the SOS recipient, and pushing firmware. On one Android watch they report system-level code execution. For SinoTrack they describe SQL injection reachable through a demo login and commands that could unlock doors or cut fuel. For TKSTAR they describe a publicly downloadable backup archive that exposed source code, hard-coded credentials, and a web shell that had sat on a server for about two years. They say they filed 45 CVEs and got little substantive vendor response.

The takeaway is that brand variety hides a shared supply chain, so one flaw can affect many products at once. The speakers urge owners to stop using these devices and argue that basic practices, such as removing hard-coded secrets, validating TLS, parameterizing SQL, and hashing passwords, would have blocked most of the findings.

talks.title: This Message Was Sent by Microsoft - Turning First Party Services into our Phishing Platform
talks.teaser: Shows how notification features in first-party Microsoft services can be abused to send custom phishing pretexts from trusted Microsoft addresses.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from last year's research, when custom CSS on the Microsoft sign-in page let a phishing login look genuine. Microsoft has since blocked those CSS techniques. This year the speaker asked whether an attacker could move earlier in the chain and have Microsoft's own mail systems deliver the phishing message.

The speaker tested several built-in notification features. Azure DevOps work items let an attacker control the subject and much of the body, though default links and boilerplate had to be hidden with injected CSS. Power BI report subscriptions and the SharePoint share-by-email API gave fuller control over content. Weak recipient validation allowed external addresses, and removing licenses let the sender display name match addresses such as billing or HR on Microsoft domains. The most effective case was Entra ID adaptive cards, which render interactive forms inside the mail client. Registering an originator and getting a global provider approved let the speaker collect passwords in the message itself and then relay an MFA prompt to the victim.

Microsoft's responses were mixed. The Azure DevOps report was ruled out of bounty scope but still fixed, and the speaker reports that the global provider was approved within two days. The main takeaway is that a message with valid SPF, DKIM and DMARC from a Microsoft address does not prove it came from Microsoft's customer or from the sender it claims. Defenders should treat SaaS notification abuse as a real phishing vector and review how external recipients and interactive cards are handled in their tenants.

talks.title: Cracking North Korea's Info Control - Breaking Open the World's Most Locked-Down Information System
talks.teaser: Maps North Korea's state surveillance stack, from signature-enforced Android phones to Windows concealment, and the engineering gaps for information-access tools.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a technologist from Liberty in North Korea describing how the state controls information. Domestic phones are rebranded Chinese handsets running a custom Android build with no app store. Apps and files must carry state-issued cryptographic signatures. A background service called TraceViewer takes screenshots every five minutes and on file events, and its companion RedFlag deletes any file or APK that lacks a valid signature. The national network is tiny, reachable through two egress points, and desktops often run an old input method that disables UAC.

The middle section walks through the signature format and an emulator demo in which an unsigned image is removed on transfer while a camera photo gets signed on the device. Older handsets still allowed boot ROM and fastboot access, but newer models locked these down. Chip-off attempts on two devices failed. A leaked signing tool is shown applying a self-signed block bound to a chosen IMEI. The speaker also covers smuggling through USB drives, micro SD cards, DVD-style players and smart TVs, and how ordinary cleaning utilities are used to hide activity from inspectors.

The closing part is a call for help. Funding for NGOs has dropped, and the group relies on defector testing for every product. It lists open needs including encrypted messaging, Android exploitation, embedded work, censorship bypass and distribution networks, and invites practitioners to get in touch.
